entry.sum: A commutative ring is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated, or equivalently if every ascending chain of ideals $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$ eventually stops. Hilbert's basis theorem says that $R[x]$ is Noetherian whenever $R$ is, so every ideal of $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ has finitely many generators and every system of polynomial equations is equivalent to a finite one.
key: I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots \implies I_N = I_{N+1} = \cdots \text{ for some } N
R \text{ Noetherian} \implies R[x_1, \dots, x_n] \text{ Noetherian}
R \text{ Noetherian},\ I \text{ an ideal} \implies R/I \text{ Noetherian}
entry.why: It is the finiteness condition behind most of commutative algebra and algebraic geometry: it guarantees that zero sets of polynomials have finite descriptions and that procedures such as Buchberger's Gröbner basis algorithm terminate.

links.note: Rings of integers of number fields are Noetherian, which is one of the three conditions in the definition of a Dedekind domain, where ideals factor uniquely into prime ideals.
Termination of Buchberger's algorithm for Gröbner bases, the core of computer algebra systems, follows from the ascending chain condition on monomial ideals.

refs: Atiyah & Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra
Dummit & Foote, Abstract Algebra
Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry

blocks.body:
Suppose someone hands you an infinite list of polynomial equations in three unknowns, say $f_1 = 0, f_2 = 0, f_3 = 0, \dots$, and asks for the common solutions. Is the infinite list really needed, or could you always throw away all but finitely many equations without changing the answer? In 1890 Hilbert proved that a finite sub-list always suffices. The algebraic property behind this is called being Noetherian, after Emmy Noether, who saw that one simple finiteness condition on ideals drives a large part of commutative algebra.

This page gives three equivalent definitions, proves Hilbert's basis theorem, and shows what the condition buys. Throughout, ring means commutative ring with $1$, as on the page on [[rings]].

In the integers every ideal has the form $(n) = n\mathbb{Z}$, so one generator is enough. The same is true in $k[x]$ for a field $k$, because both rings are principal ideal domains: an ideal is generated by any of its nonzero elements of smallest size (absolute value, or degree).

For two variables this fails: the ideal $(x, y) \subseteq k[x,y]$ of polynomials with zero constant term is not principal. A single generator $g$ would have to divide both $x$ and $y$, forcing $g$ to be a nonzero constant, but then $(g)$ would be the whole ring, which contains $1 \notin (x,y)$. Still, two generators suffice. The question is whether some finite number of generators always suffices.

It does not in every ring. Let $R = k[x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots]$ be the polynomial ring in infinitely many variables (each polynomial uses only finitely many of them). The ideal $I = (x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots)$ is not finitely generated: finitely many elements of $I$ involve only $x_1, \dots, x_n$ for some $n$, and we will see in Example 1 that $x_{n+1}$ is then not in the ideal they generate. Equivalently, the chain
$$(x_1) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2, x_3) \subsetneq \cdots$$
climbs forever. These two symptoms, an ideal needing infinitely many generators and an ascending chain of ideals that never stops, turn out to be the same disease.

blocks.title: Noetherian ring
Equivalence of the three conditions
blocks.body: For a ring $R$, the three conditions in the definition are equivalent.

(1) implies (2). Let $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be a chain and let $I = \bigcup_n I_n$. This union is an ideal: if $a, b \in I$ then $a \in I_m$ and $b \in I_n$, and both lie in $I_{\max(m,n)}$, so $a - b$ and $ra$ lie in $I$. By (1), $I = (a_1, \dots, a_r)$. Each $a_j$ lies in some $I_{n_j}$; put $N = \max_j n_j$. Then all $a_j \in I_N$, so $I \subseteq I_N \subseteq I_n \subseteq I$ for every $n \ge N$, and the chain is constant from $N$ on.

(2) implies (3). Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a nonempty collection of ideals with no maximal element. Pick $I_1 \in \mathcal{S}$. Since $I_1$ is not maximal in $\mathcal{S}$ there is $I_2 \in \mathcal{S}$ with $I_1 \subsetneq I_2$, then $I_3 \in \mathcal{S}$ with $I_2 \subsetneq I_3$, and so on. This chain never stabilises, contradicting (2).

(3) implies (1). Let $I$ be an ideal and let $\mathcal{S}$ be the collection of finitely generated ideals contained in $I$. It is nonempty, since $(0) \in \mathcal{S}$, so it has a maximal element $J = (a_1, \dots, a_r)$. If some $a \in I$ were not in $J$, then $(a_1, \dots, a_r, a)$ would be a finitely generated ideal inside $I$ strictly larger than $J$, contradicting maximality. Hence $I = J$ is finitely generated.

Fields and principal ideal domains such as $\mathbb{Z}$, $k[x]$ and the Gaussian integers are Noetherian, since every ideal has one generator. Two closure properties make it easy to produce many more examples.

Quotients. If $R$ is Noetherian and $I$ is an ideal, then $R/I$ is Noetherian. The ideals of $R/I$ correspond, preserving inclusion, to the ideals of $R$ that contain $I$ (the correspondence theorem from [[rings]]), so an ascending chain in $R/I$ lifts to an ascending chain in $R$, which stops.

Polynomial rings. This is Hilbert's theorem, proved below: if $R$ is Noetherian, so is $R[x]$. By induction, $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian. Combining the two properties, every ring of the form $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]/I$ is Noetherian; these are exactly the rings generated over $R$ by finitely many elements. So $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] \cong \mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2+5)$, $\mathbb{C}[x,y]/(y^2 - x^3)$ and every ring of integers of a number field are Noetherian.

blocks.title: Hilbert's basis theorem
blocks.body: If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring $R[x]$ is Noetherian. Consequently $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian, and in particular every ideal of $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ ($k$ a field) and of $\mathbb{Z}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is finitely generated.

blocks.title: Proof of Hilbert's basis theorem
blocks.body:
The idea is to control an ideal of $R[x]$ through the leading coefficients of its elements, which live in the Noetherian ring $R$.

Suppose some ideal $I \subseteq R[x]$ is not finitely generated. Choose $f_1 \in I$ of smallest possible degree among nonzero elements of $I$. Having chosen $f_1, \dots, f_k$, the ideal $(f_1, \dots, f_k)$ is not all of $I$, so choose $f_{k+1} \in I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_k)$ of smallest possible degree. Let $d_k = \deg f_k$ and let $a_k \in R$ be the leading coefficient of $f_k$.

The degrees never decrease: $f_{k+1}$ was available at the previous step as well (it lies in $I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_{k-1})$), so $d_k \le d_{k+1}$ by the minimal choice of $f_k$.

Now look at the chain of ideals of $R$
$$(a_1) \subseteq (a_1, a_2) \subseteq (a_1, a_2, a_3) \subseteq \cdots .$$
Since $R$ is Noetherian it stabilises, so for some $N$ we have $a_{N+1} \in (a_1, \dots, a_N)$, say $a_{N+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i a_i$ with $r_i \in R$. Consider
$$g = f_{N+1} - \sum_{i=1}^{N} r_i\, x^{d_{N+1} - d_i} f_i .$$
The exponents $d_{N+1} - d_i$ are nonnegative because the degrees are nondecreasing. Each term $r_i x^{d_{N+1}-d_i} f_i$ has degree at most $d_{N+1}$ with coefficient $r_i a_i$ in degree $d_{N+1}$, so the coefficient of $x^{d_{N+1}}$ in $g$ is $a_{N+1} - \sum r_i a_i = 0$, and $\deg g < d_{N+1}$ (or $g = 0$).

But $g \in I$, and $g \notin (f_1, \dots, f_N)$: otherwise $f_{N+1} = g + \sum r_i x^{d_{N+1}-d_i} f_i$ would lie in $(f_1, \dots, f_N)$. In particular $g \neq 0$. So $g$ is an element of $I \setminus (f_1, \dots, f_N)$ of degree smaller than $d_{N+1}$, contradicting the choice of $f_{N+1}$. Hence every ideal of $R[x]$ is finitely generated.

The consequences follow by induction, since $R[x_1, \dots, x_n] = (R[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}])[x_n]$, starting from the Noetherian rings $k$ and $\mathbb{Z}$.

blocks.title: What the theorem says about equations
blocks.body:
Back to the opening question. For a set $S$ of polynomials in $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$, write $V(S)$ for the set of common zeros in $k^n$. If $I$ is the ideal generated by $S$, then $V(S) = V(I)$, because any combination $\sum h_i s_i$ vanishes wherever all the $s_i$ do. By Hilbert's theorem $I = (g_1, \dots, g_r)$, and each $g_j$ is itself a combination of finitely many elements of $S$. Collecting those finitely many elements $s_1, \dots, s_m$ we get $I = (s_1, \dots, s_m)$ and therefore
$$V(S) = V(s_1, \dots, s_m).$$
Every system of polynomial equations, however large, is equivalent to a finite subsystem.

The ascending chain condition on ideals turns into a descending chain condition on solution sets: if $V_1 \supseteq V_2 \supseteq \cdots$ are zero sets of polynomials, the corresponding ideals of vanishing polynomials increase, hence stop, and so the $V_i$ stop shrinking. From this one proves that every algebraic set is a finite union of irreducible pieces, the first structural fact of algebraic geometry.

There is also an algorithmic side. Buchberger's algorithm for Gröbner bases repeatedly adds new polynomials to a list; it terminates because the ideals generated by the leading terms form an ascending chain, which must stop. Dickson's lemma (Example 3) is the monomial version of the same phenomenon.

blocks.title: Noetherian modules and further results
blocks.body:
The same finiteness makes sense for modules, the setting of [[modules]]. An $R$-module $M$ is Noetherian if every submodule is finitely generated, equivalently if ascending chains of submodules stop; a ring is Noetherian exactly when it is Noetherian as a module over itself, since its submodules are its ideals.

A standard lemma, stated here without proof: if $N \subseteq M$ is a submodule, then $M$ is Noetherian if and only if both $N$ and $M/N$ are. From this, by induction, $R^n$ is Noetherian when $R$ is, and so is every quotient of $R^n$, that is, every finitely generated $R$-module. So over a Noetherian ring, submodules of finitely generated modules are again finitely generated. For $R = \mathbb{Z}$ this says that subgroups of finitely generated abelian groups are finitely generated, a fact used silently in the structure theorem.

Primary decomposition of ideals (the Lasker–Noether theorem), Krull's intersection theorem and dimension theory all assume the Noetherian condition. Hilbert's theorem also has a power series version (again stated without proof): if $R$ is Noetherian, so is the power series ring $R[\![x]\!]$.

blocks.title: Example 1: infinitely many variables
blocks.body: Show that in $R = k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ the chain $(x_1) \subseteq (x_1, x_2) \subseteq \cdots$ is strictly increasing, so $R$ is not Noetherian.
blocks.solution:
Fix $n$ and suppose $x_{n+1} \in (x_1, \dots, x_n)$, say $x_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} h_i x_i$ with $h_i \in R$. Apply the ring homomorphism $\varphi\colon R \to R$ that sends $x_1, \dots, x_n$ to $0$ and fixes every other variable (substitution is a ring homomorphism). The right-hand side maps to $\sum \varphi(h_i)\cdot 0 = 0$, while the left-hand side maps to $x_{n+1} \ne 0$. Contradiction.

So $x_{n+1} \notin (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and each inclusion is strict. The chain never stabilises, condition (2) fails, and $R$ is not Noetherian. (The same substitution shows that the ideal $(x_1, x_2, \dots)$ is not finitely generated.)

blocks.title: Example 2: a monomial ideal
blocks.body: In $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ let $I$ be the ideal generated by all monomials $x^i y^j$ with $i + 2j \ge 4$. Hilbert's theorem promises finitely many generators. Find them.
blocks.solution:
First a general fact. If $I$ is generated by a set of monomials, then a monomial $m$ lies in $I$ exactly when some generating monomial divides it. Indeed if $m = \sum h_k m_k$, expand every $h_k$ into monomials: each monomial appearing on the right is a multiple of some $m_k$, and $m$ itself must appear on the right after cancellation, so $m$ is a multiple of some $m_k$.

So we only need the monomials in the set that are not divisible by another one in the set: the minimal exponent pairs $(i,j)$ with $i + 2j \ge 4$ under the componentwise order. For $j = 0$ the smallest $i$ is $4$; for $j = 1$ it is $i = 2$; for $j = 2$ it is $i = 0$. Any pair with $j \ge 2$ dominates $(0,2)$, any pair with $j=1$ dominates $(2,1)$, and any pair with $j=0$ dominates $(4,0)$. Hence
$$I = (x^4,\ x^2 y,\ y^2).$$
Three generators replace infinitely many. Notice that the minimal generating set of a monomial ideal is unique, though ideals in general have many different generating sets.

blocks.title: Example 3: Dickson's lemma from the ascending chain condition
blocks.body: (Dickson's lemma, olympiad style.) Prove that in any infinite sequence $(a_1, b_1), (a_2, b_2), \dots$ of pairs of nonnegative integers there are indices $i < j$ with $a_i \le a_j$ and $b_i \le b_j$.
blocks.solution:
Encode the pairs as monomials $m_k = x^{a_k} y^{b_k}$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ and consider the ideals $J_k = (m_1, \dots, m_k)$. These form an ascending chain, so by Hilbert's theorem and condition (2) there is $N$ with $J_{N+1} = J_N$. Then $m_{N+1} \in (m_1, \dots, m_N)$, and by the fact from Example 2 some $m_i$ with $i \le N$ divides $m_{N+1}$, which means exactly $a_i \le a_{N+1}$ and $b_i \le b_{N+1}$. Take $j = N+1$.

The same argument works verbatim for $n$-tuples, using $\mathbb{Q}[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. (There is also an elementary proof by extracting nondecreasing subsequences coordinate by coordinate.)

blocks.body:
- A subring of a Noetherian ring can fail to be Noetherian: $k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is not Noetherian, yet it lies inside its field of fractions, which has only two ideals. Another classic example is the ring of rational polynomials with integer constant term, $\mathbb{Z} + x\mathbb{Q}[x]$, inside $\mathbb{Q}[x]$: there the chain $(x) \subsetneq (x/2) \subsetneq (x/4) \subsetneq \cdots$ never stops.
- Noetherian does not mean a bounded number of generators. In $k[x,y]$ the ideal $(x,y)^n$ needs $n+1$ generators $x^n, x^{n-1}y, \dots, y^n$, so no single bound works for all ideals.
- The ascending chain condition does not imply the descending one: in $\mathbb{Z}$ the chain $(2) \supsetneq (4) \supsetneq (8) \supsetneq \cdots$ never stops. Rings with the descending chain condition (Artinian rings) form a much smaller class.
- Being a UFD and being Noetherian are independent: $k[x_1, x_2, \dots]$ is a UFD but not Noetherian, and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is Noetherian but not a UFD.

Principal ideal domains such as those on [[ufds]] and [[gaussian-integers]] are the simplest Noetherian rings. In algebraic number theory, rings of integers are Noetherian domains in which nonzero ideals factor uniquely into primes; see [[ideals]] and [[class-group]]. In algebraic geometry, Hilbert's basis theorem is what makes zero sets of polynomials manageable, and the Nullstellensatz (also due to Hilbert) then matches them with radical ideals. The modules side continues the theory on [[modules]], and the leading-coefficient idea of the proof reappears in Gröbner basis algorithms, a topic close to [[algorithms]]. The same ascending chain condition, applied to the open sets of a space, gives the notion of a Noetherian topological space, a variant of the ideas on [[topological-spaces]].

2. Find the minimal monomial generators of the ideal of $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ generated by all $x^i y^j$ with $ij \ge 6$.

entry.sum: A category consists of objects and composable arrows (morphisms) with identities, subject to associativity; a functor maps objects to objects and arrows to arrows, preserving composition; a natural transformation $\eta\colon F \Rightarrow G$ is a family of arrows $\eta_X\colon F(X) \to G(X)$ compatible with every arrow $f\colon X \to Y$. The one idea to remember: study objects through the maps between them, and call a construction natural when it commutes with all maps.
key: (h \circ g) \circ f = h \circ (g \circ f), \qquad f \circ \mathrm{id}_X = f = \mathrm{id}_Y \circ f
\eta_Y \circ F(f) = G(f) \circ \eta_X \quad \text{for all } f\colon X \to Y
\mathrm{Nat}\big(\mathrm{Hom}(A,-), F\big) \cong F(A) \quad \text{(Yoneda)}
entry.why: Functoriality turns topology into algebra: because the fundamental group is a functor, the disc cannot retract onto its boundary circle. Universal properties and the Yoneda lemma explain why products, tensor products and free objects are unique up to unique isomorphism.

links.note: Algebraic topology is built on functors such as the fundamental group and homology, which send homeomorphic spaces to isomorphic groups and so detect when spaces differ.
In typed functional programming, type constructors with a mapping operation are functors, and the semantics of typed lambda calculi is given in cartesian closed categories.
Modern algebraic geometry describes schemes through the functors they represent and uses sheaves, which are contravariant functors on the open sets of a space satisfying a gluing condition.

Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician
Leinster, Basic Category Theory

blocks.body:
Every course in algebra or topology builds the same constructions again and again. The product of two groups, of two vector spaces and of two topological spaces are each defined separately, yet in each case the product is the thing with two projection maps through which every pair of maps factors uniquely. A finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to its dual and to its double dual, yet every textbook insists that the second isomorphism is "natural" and the first is not. What do these words mean?

Category theory gives the precise language. Its basic idea is to study objects through the maps between them. A category records objects and maps, a functor is a map between categories, and a natural transformation is a map between functors; with these, "natural" becomes a definition. The examples come from [[groups]], [[vector-spaces]] and [[topological-spaces]].

blocks.title: Category
Examples of categories
blocks.body:
The familiar categories have structured sets as objects and structure-preserving functions as morphisms: $\mathbf{Set}$ (sets and all functions), $\mathbf{Grp}$ (groups and homomorphisms), $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ (vector spaces over $k$ and linear maps), $\mathbf{Top}$ (topological spaces and continuous maps). In each, composition is composition of functions, which is automatically associative.

But morphisms need not be functions, and some of the most useful small examples look nothing like these.

- A partially ordered set $(P, \le)$ is a category: the objects are the elements, and there is exactly one morphism $x \to y$ when $x \le y$ and none otherwise. Reflexivity gives identities and transitivity gives composition.
- A group $G$ is a category with a single object $\ast$, whose morphisms $\ast \to \ast$ are the elements of $G$ and whose composition is the group operation. In this category every morphism is an isomorphism.
- The matrix category over a field $k$ has the natural numbers $0, 1, 2, \dots$ as objects, $m \times n$ matrices as the morphisms $n \to m$, and matrix multiplication as composition; the identity matrix $I_n$ is $\mathrm{id}_n$.

Because a category is described entirely by arrows, a definition that uses only arrows makes sense in every category at once. For example, a product of $X$ and $Y$ is an object $P$ with morphisms $p_1\colon P \to X$, $p_2\colon P \to Y$ such that for every pair $f\colon T \to X$, $g\colon T \to Y$ there is exactly one $h\colon T \to P$ with $p_1 \circ h = f$ and $p_2 \circ h = g$. In $\mathbf{Set}$, $\mathbf{Grp}$, $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ and $\mathbf{Top}$ this produces the Cartesian product, the direct product, the direct sum and the product topology. In a poset it produces the greatest lower bound. Any two products of $X$ and $Y$ are isomorphic by a unique isomorphism compatible with the projections, which is why one says "the" product.

blocks.title: Functor
blocks.body:
A (covariant) functor $F\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$ an object $F(X)$ of $\mathcal{D}$, and to each morphism $f\colon X \to Y$ a morphism $F(f)\colon F(X) \to F(Y)$, such that
$$F(g \circ f) = F(g) \circ F(f), \qquad F(\mathrm{id}_X) = \mathrm{id}_{F(X)}.$$
A contravariant functor is the same except that it reverses arrows: $F(f)\colon F(Y) \to F(X)$ and $F(g \circ f) = F(f) \circ F(g)$.

A functor is a construction that applies not only to objects but also to maps, compatibly with composition.

blocks.title: Examples of functors
blocks.body:
- Forgetful functors, such as $U\colon \mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Set}$, send a group to its underlying set and a homomorphism to the same function.
- The free vector space functor $\mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Vect}_k$ sends a set $S$ to the space with basis $S$, and a function to the linear map that does the same thing to basis vectors.
- Abelianisation $G \mapsto G^{\mathrm{ab}} = G/[G,G]$ is a functor $\mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Grp}$: a homomorphism $\varphi\colon G \to H$ maps commutators to commutators, so it induces $G^{\mathrm{ab}} \to H^{\mathrm{ab}}$.
- The dual space $V \mapsto V^* = \mathrm{Hom}(V, k)$ is contravariant: a linear map $f\colon V \to W$ induces $f^*\colon W^* \to V^*$, $f^*(\psi) = \psi \circ f$, and $(g \circ f)^* = f^* \circ g^*$.
- For a fixed object $A$, the hom functor $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -)\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ sends $X$ to $\mathrm{Hom}(A, X)$ and $f\colon X \to Y$ to the function $u \mapsto f \circ u$.
- The fundamental group sends a pointed space $(X, x_0)$ to the group $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ and a continuous pointed map to the induced homomorphism of loops; see [[fundamental-group]]. Homology groups are functors in the same way; see [[homology]].
- A functor from a group regarded as a one-object category to $\mathbf{Vect}_k$ is exactly a representation of the group; see [[group-representations]].

The first payoff of the definition costs one line.

blocks.title: Functors preserve isomorphisms
blocks.body: Every functor sends isomorphisms to isomorphisms. Consequently, if $F(X)$ and $F(Y)$ are not isomorphic, then $X$ and $Y$ are not isomorphic.

If $g \circ f = \mathrm{id}_X$ and $f \circ g = \mathrm{id}_Y$, then $F(g) \circ F(f) = F(g \circ f) = F(\mathrm{id}_X) = \mathrm{id}_{F(X)}$, and likewise $F(f) \circ F(g) = \mathrm{id}_{F(Y)}$. (For a contravariant functor the same computation works with the order reversed.)

blocks.title: Natural transformation
blocks.body:
Let $F, G\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{D}$ be functors. A natural transformation $\eta\colon F \Rightarrow G$ is a family of morphisms $\eta_X\colon F(X) \to G(X)$ in $\mathcal{D}$, one for each object $X$ of $\mathcal{C}$, such that for every morphism $f\colon X \to Y$
$$\eta_Y \circ F(f) = G(f) \circ \eta_X .$$
It is a natural isomorphism if every component $\eta_X$ is an isomorphism.

The condition (often drawn as a commuting square) says that $\eta$ is given by one uniform rule that does not depend on arbitrary choices made separately for each object: transporting along $f$ and then applying $\eta$ gives the same result as applying $\eta$ and then transporting.

blocks.title: Example 1: the double dual is natural
blocks.body: For a vector space $V$ over $k$, let $\mathrm{ev}_V\colon V \to V^{**}$ be evaluation, $\mathrm{ev}_V(v)(\varphi) = \varphi(v)$. Show that $\mathrm{ev}$ is a natural transformation from the identity functor to the double dual functor $V \mapsto V^{**}$ (which is covariant, being contravariant twice).
blocks.solution:
Let $f\colon V \to W$ be linear. The double dual functor sends it to $f^{**}\colon V^{**} \to W^{**}$, $f^{**}(\Theta) = \Theta \circ f^*$. We must check $\mathrm{ev}_W \circ f = f^{**} \circ \mathrm{ev}_V$. Apply both sides to $v \in V$ and then to $\psi \in W^*$:
$$\big(f^{**}(\mathrm{ev}_V(v))\big)(\psi) = \mathrm{ev}_V(v)\big(f^*\psi\big) = (\psi \circ f)(v) = \psi(f(v)) = \mathrm{ev}_W(f(v))(\psi).$$
So the square commutes for every $f$. No basis was used. For finite-dimensional $V$ each $\mathrm{ev}_V$ is injective (a nonzero $v$ extends to a basis, and the coordinate functional of $v$ does not vanish on it) between spaces of equal dimension, hence an isomorphism. So, on finite-dimensional spaces, $\mathrm{ev}$ is a natural isomorphism; see [[dual-spaces]].

blocks.title: Example 2: the dual is not naturally isomorphic
blocks.body: A finite-dimensional space is also isomorphic to its dual $V^*$, by sending a basis to the dual basis. Show that no such isomorphism can be chosen naturally, even if we only ask for compatibility with invertible maps. Precisely: work over $\mathbb{Q}$ and suppose that for each finite-dimensional $V$ we have an isomorphism $\eta_V\colon V \to V^*$ with $f^* \circ \eta_W \circ f = \eta_V$ for every invertible linear $f\colon V \to W$. Derive a contradiction.
blocks.solution:
(The condition $f^* \circ \eta_W \circ f = \eta_V$ is the natural form of the requirement, since $V \mapsto V^*$ reverses arrows.) Take $V = W = \mathbb{Q}$ and $f$ = multiplication by $2$. A linear map $\eta\colon \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}^*$ has the form $\eta(v)(w) = a v w$ for a fixed scalar $a$, and it is an isomorphism exactly when $a \ne 0$.

Compute the left-hand side: $(f^* \circ \eta \circ f)(v)$ is the functional $w \mapsto \eta(f v)(f w) = a (2v)(2w) = 4 a v w$. The condition demands $4a = a$, so $a = 0$, and $\eta_{\mathbb{Q}}$ is not an isomorphism. Contradiction.

So every isomorphism $V \cong V^*$ depends on a choice (a basis, or an inner product), whereas $V \cong V^{**}$ does not.

blocks.title: Yoneda lemma
blocks.body:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category, $A$ an object, and $F\colon \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ a functor. The map
$$\mathrm{Nat}\big(\mathrm{Hom}(A, -), F\big) \to F(A), \qquad \eta \mapsto \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$$
is a bijection. Its inverse sends $x \in F(A)$ to the transformation with components $\eta_X(u) = F(u)(x)$ for $u\colon A \to X$.

Given $x \in F(A)$, define $\eta^x_X(u) = F(u)(x)$. This is natural: for $f\colon X \to Y$ and $u \in \mathrm{Hom}(A, X)$,
$$\eta^x_Y(f \circ u) = F(f \circ u)(x) = F(f)\big(F(u)(x)\big) = F(f)\big(\eta^x_X(u)\big).$$
And $\eta^x_A(\mathrm{id}_A) = F(\mathrm{id}_A)(x) = x$, so $x \mapsto \eta^x$ followed by $\eta \mapsto \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$ is the identity.

Conversely let $\eta$ be any natural transformation and $x = \eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)$. For $u\colon A \to X$, naturality applied to the morphism $u$ and the element $\mathrm{id}_A$ gives
$$\eta_X(u) = \eta_X(u \circ \mathrm{id}_A) = F(u)\big(\eta_A(\mathrm{id}_A)\big) = F(u)(x) = \eta^x_X(u).$$
So $\eta = \eta^x$, and the two maps are mutually inverse.

blocks.title: What the Yoneda lemma means, and adjunctions
blocks.body:
The Yoneda lemma says that a natural transformation out of $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -)$ is completely determined by where it sends the single element $\mathrm{id}_A$. Taking $F = \mathrm{Hom}(B, -)$, one deduces that natural transformations $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-) \Rightarrow \mathrm{Hom}(B,-)$ correspond to morphisms $B \to A$, and hence that $A \cong B$ as soon as $\mathrm{Hom}(A, -) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(B, -)$ naturally. An object is determined up to isomorphism by the maps out of it. This is the precise form of the slogan at the start, and it is why universal properties (which describe hom sets) determine objects.

A related key notion is adjunction. The free group functor $F\colon \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Grp}$ and the forgetful functor $U$ satisfy
$$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Grp}}(F(S), G) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Set}}(S, U(G)),$$
naturally in both $S$ and $G$: a homomorphism out of a free group is the same as an arbitrary function on its generators. One says $F$ is left adjoint to $U$. Free modules, abelianisation, tensor products ([[tensor-products]]) and the Stone–Čech compactification are all adjoints, and a general theorem (stated here without proof) says that left adjoints preserve colimits (such as quotients and direct sums) and right adjoints preserve limits (such as products and kernels).

blocks.title: Example 3: counting functors between posets
blocks.body: Regard the chain $0 < 1 < 2$ as a category $\mathbf{3}$. How many functors $\mathbf{3} \to \mathbf{3}$ are there? How many natural transformations are there from the identity functor to the constant functor at $2$, and from the constant functor at $2$ to the identity?
blocks.solution:
In a poset category there is at most one morphism between two objects. So a functor is determined by its values on objects, $i \mapsto F(i)$, and it exists precisely when every morphism $i \to j$ (that is, every $i \le j$) has somewhere to go, namely $F(i) \le F(j)$. Composition and identities are then preserved automatically, because there is only one possible arrow. Functors between posets are exactly order-preserving maps.

Counting nondecreasing maps $\{0,1,2\} \to \{0,1,2\}$: such a map is determined by how many of the three inputs go to each output, which is a way of writing $3$ as an ordered sum of three nonnegative parts. By stars and bars there are $\binom{3+2}{2} = 10$ of them.

A natural transformation $\eta\colon F \Rightarrow G$ between such functors needs a morphism $F(i) \to G(i)$ for every $i$, i.e. $F(i) \le G(i)$; the naturality squares commute automatically, again because parallel arrows in a poset are equal. From the identity to the constant functor $2$ we need $i \le 2$ for all $i$: exactly one transformation. In the other direction we need $2 \le i$ for all $i$, which fails at $i = 0$: none. So between poset-valued functors there is at most one natural transformation, and it exists iff $F \le G$ pointwise.

blocks.title: Example 4: a functor proves a topological fact
blocks.body: Use the fundamental group functor to show that there is no continuous map $r\colon D^2 \to S^1$ from the closed disc to its boundary circle with $r(z) = z$ for all $z \in S^1$ (a retraction).
blocks.solution:
Let $i\colon S^1 \to D^2$ be the inclusion. A retraction would satisfy $r \circ i = \mathrm{id}_{S^1}$. Apply the functor $\pi_1$ (with base point $1 \in S^1$):
$$\pi_1(r) \circ \pi_1(i) = \pi_1(r \circ i) = \pi_1(\mathrm{id}_{S^1}) = \mathrm{id}_{\pi_1(S^1)}.$$
Now $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_1(D^2)$ is trivial, since the disc is convex and every loop contracts by straight-line homotopy. So the identity of $\mathbb{Z}$ factors through the trivial group, $\mathbb{Z} \to 1 \to \mathbb{Z}$, which is impossible because such a composite sends $1$ to $0$. This is the core of Brouwer's fixed point theorem in dimension $2$.

blocks.body:
- A functor must act on morphisms, not only on objects, and must respect composition. The centre $G \mapsto Z(G)$ is a perfectly good rule on objects but is not a functor on $\mathbf{Grp}$ (see the exercises).
- Naturality is a property of a whole family, not of each component. Every $V$ is isomorphic to $V^*$; what fails is the existence of a family of such isomorphisms compatible with all maps.
- In a general category, morphisms need not be functions and objects need not have elements, so arguments like "pick $x \in X$" do not make sense in a poset or a one-object category.
- The objects of $\mathbf{Set}$ do not form a set (there is no set of all sets). Categories whose objects form a set are called small; the distinction matters when forming functor categories or applying the Yoneda lemma to large categories.

Functors are the organising principle of algebraic topology: [[fundamental-group]] and [[homology]] are functors from spaces to groups, and their functoriality is what turns computations into impossibility proofs. In algebra, [[tensor-products]] and [[dual-spaces]] are best understood through universal properties and natural isomorphisms, and modules over a ring form a category with kernels and cokernels; see [[modules]]. Representations of a group are functors out of the group regarded as a category; see [[group-representations]]. Taking derivatives at base points is a functor on pointed [[smooth-manifolds|smooth manifolds]], and passing from a Lie group to its Lie algebra is a functor on [[lie-groups|Lie groups]]. In logic and computer science, categories model types and programs, and the internal logic of a category connects with [[logic-basics]].

1. Show that the vertical composite of two natural transformations $F \Rightarrow G \Rightarrow H$ is a natural transformation.
2. Show that the quotient maps $G \to G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ form a natural transformation from the identity functor on $\mathbf{Grp}$ to abelianisation.
3. Let $i\colon \mathbb{Z}/2 \to S_3$ send the generator to a transposition and let $\mathrm{sgn}\colon S_3 \to \mathbb{Z}/2$ be the sign. Use $\mathrm{sgn} \circ i = \mathrm{id}$ and $Z(S_3) = 1$ to show that there is no functor $F\colon \mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Grp}$ with $F(G) = Z(G)$ for every group $G$, however $F$ is defined on morphisms.
4. In a poset regarded as a category, show that the product of $x$ and $y$, when it exists, is their greatest lower bound.

entry.sum: A representation of a group $G$ is a homomorphism $\rho\colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$, a way for $G$ to act on a vector space by invertible linear maps. For a finite group over $\mathbb{C}$, Maschke's theorem says every representation splits as a direct sum of irreducible ones, because averaging over $G$ produces an invariant inner product, and Schur's lemma says the only maps between irreducibles that respect the action are $0$, isomorphisms and scalars.
key: \rho(gh) = \rho(g)\rho(h), \qquad \langle u, v \rangle_G = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\langle \rho(g)u, \rho(g)v \rangle
V = V_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_r \text{ with each } V_i \text{ irreducible} \quad (G \text{ finite},\ \mathbb{C})
T \in \mathrm{Hom}_G(V, V),\ V \text{ irreducible over } \mathbb{C} \implies T = \lambda I
entry.why: Linear problems with symmetry, such as the vibration modes of a symmetric molecule or a random walk on a group, decompose into independent pieces indexed by irreducible representations; for cyclic groups this decomposition is the discrete Fourier transform.

links.note: Fourier analysis on a finite abelian group is the decomposition of functions on the group into its $1$-dimensional representations, and the non-abelian version uses all irreducible representations.
Mixing times of random walks on groups, such as card shuffling on $S_n$, can be bounded by decomposing the walk's transition operator over the irreducible representations of the group.

refs: Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups
Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course
James & Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups

blocks.body:
The symmetric group $S_3$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^3$ by permuting coordinates. Two subspaces are left alone by every permutation: the line $L$ spanned by $(1,1,1)$ and the plane $P = \{x + y + z = 0\}$. Since $\mathbb{C}^3 = L \oplus P$, the action splits into a $1$-dimensional piece where $S_3$ does nothing and a $2$-dimensional piece which, as we will check, cannot be split any further.

Representation theory studies a group through the ways it can act by linear maps, and asks this question in general: can every linear action of a finite group be cut into indivisible pieces, and what are the pieces? For finite groups over $\mathbb{C}$ the answer is a clean yes (Maschke's theorem), and the pieces obey strong rules (Schur's lemma). Linear algebra then gives information about the group, and the group gives information about linear problems with symmetry, from vibrating molecules to Fourier analysis. The page uses [[group-actions]] and [[inner-products]].

blocks.title: Representation
blocks.body:
A representation of a group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ is a group homomorphism
$$\rho\colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V), \qquad \rho(gh) = \rho(g)\rho(h).$$
The dimension of $V$ is the degree of $\rho$. A subspace $W \subseteq V$ is invariant (a subrepresentation) if $\rho(g)W \subseteq W$ for all $g$. A representation $V \neq 0$ is irreducible if its only invariant subspaces are $0$ and $V$. Two representations $(\rho, V)$ and $(\sigma, W)$ are equivalent (isomorphic) if there is a linear isomorphism $T\colon V \to W$ with $T\rho(g) = \sigma(g)T$ for all $g$; more generally a linear map with this property is called a $G$-map or intertwiner.

Choosing a basis turns a representation into a homomorphism into invertible $n \times n$ matrices; equivalent representations are the same up to a change of basis.

blocks.title: First examples
blocks.body:
- The trivial representation: $V = \mathbb{C}$ and $\rho(g) = 1$ for all $g$.
- The sign representation of $S_n$: $\rho(\sigma) = \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma) = \pm 1$ on $\mathbb{C}$.
- The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n$ on $\mathbb{C}$: $\rho_j(k) = \omega^{jk}$ where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$ and $j$ is fixed. This is a homomorphism because $\omega^n = 1$.
- Permutation representations: if $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, let $\mathbb{C}^X$ have basis vectors $e_x$ for $x \in X$ and put $\rho(g) e_x = e_{g x}$. Each $\rho(g)$ is a permutation matrix. The opening example is $S_3$ acting on $X = \{1,2,3\}$.
- The regular representation: the permutation representation of $G$ acting on itself by left multiplication, of degree $|G|$.
- Geometric representations: the dihedral group of the square acts on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (or $\mathbb{C}^2$) by rotations and reflections; $\mathbb{Z}/4$ acts by rotation through multiples of $90^\circ$.

Every $1$-dimensional representation is irreducible. A degree-$1$ representation is just a homomorphism $G \to \mathbb{C}^\times$, and since $\rho(g)^{|G|} = \rho(g^{|G|}) = 1$, its values are roots of unity.

blocks.title: Example 1: the 2-dimensional representation of S3
blocks.body: Show that the plane $P = \{(x,y,z) : x + y + z = 0\}$ inside the permutation representation of $S_3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ is irreducible.
blocks.solution:
$P$ is invariant because permuting coordinates does not change their sum. A proper nonzero invariant subspace of the $2$-dimensional space $P$ would be a line $\mathbb{C}v$ fixed by every $\rho(\sigma)$, so $v$ would be a common eigenvector of all the permutation matrices.

Let $t = (1\,2)$ swap the first two coordinates. On $P$ it has the eigenvector $u_1 = (1,-1,0)$ with eigenvalue $-1$ and $u_2 = (1,1,-2)$ with eigenvalue $+1$. These eigenvalues are distinct, so every eigenvector of $\rho(t)$ in $P$ is a multiple of $u_1$ or of $u_2$. Now let $s = (2\,3)$ swap the last two coordinates: $\rho(s)u_1 = (1,0,-1)$ and $\rho(s)u_2 = (1,-2,1)$, neither of which is a multiple of the vector it came from. So there is no common eigenvector, and $P$ is irreducible.

Thus $\mathbb{C}^3 = L \oplus P$ is a decomposition into irreducibles: the trivial representation plus a $2$-dimensional irreducible one, often called the standard representation of $S_3$.

blocks.title: When decomposition fails
blocks.body:
Not every representation splits into irreducibles, and the counterexamples show what the hypotheses of the main theorem are for.

The infinite group $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^2$ by $n \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} 1 & n \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The line spanned by $e_1$ is invariant, and it is the only invariant line, because the only eigenvectors of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ are multiples of $e_1$. So it has no invariant complement, and $\mathbb{C}^2$ is not a direct sum of irreducibles.

The same matrices with entries in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$ give a representation of the finite group $\mathbb{Z}/p$ on $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ (the matrix with $n = p$ is the identity mod $p$), and the same argument shows it does not split. Here the problem is that the characteristic $p$ divides $|G| = p$.

So two things matter: the group should be finite, and the field should have characteristic not dividing $|G|$. Over $\mathbb{C}$ the second condition is automatic. The key tool is averaging over the group, which needs division by $|G|$.

blocks.title: Maschke's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $V$ a finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$. Then every invariant subspace $W \subseteq V$ has an invariant complement $W'$, with $V = W \oplus W'$. Consequently $V$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations,
$$V = V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_r .$$
The same holds over any field whose characteristic does not divide $|G|$.

Start with any inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ on $V$ and average it over the group:
$$\langle u, v \rangle_G = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \langle \rho(g)u, \rho(g)v \rangle .$$
This is again an inner product: it is linear in the first variable, conjugate-symmetric, and $\langle v, v\rangle_G$ is an average of positive numbers when $v \ne 0$. It is also $G$-invariant. For $h \in G$,
$$\langle \rho(h)u, \rho(h)v \rangle_G = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \langle \rho(gh)u, \rho(gh)v \rangle = \langle u, v \rangle_G ,$$
because $g \mapsto gh$ is a bijection of $G$, so the sum is merely reordered.

Let $W' = W^\perp$ be the orthogonal complement with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G$; then $V = W \oplus W'$. To see that $W'$ is invariant, take $v \in W'$, $g \in G$, $w \in W$. By invariance of the inner product,
$$\langle \rho(g)v, w \rangle_G = \langle \rho(g^{-1})\rho(g)v, \rho(g^{-1})w \rangle_G = \langle v, \rho(g^{-1})w \rangle_G = 0,$$
since $\rho(g^{-1})w \in W$. So $\rho(g)v \in W'$.

For the consequence, induct on $\dim V$. If $V$ is irreducible we are done. Otherwise pick an invariant $W$ with $0 \ne W \ne V$, write $V = W \oplus W'$, and decompose $W$ and $W'$, both of smaller dimension.

Over a field $k$ with $\mathrm{char}\, k \nmid |G|$ there may be no inner product, but the same averaging works for projections: if $\pi\colon V \to W$ is any linear projection onto $W$, then $\pi^\circ = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \rho(g)\pi\rho(g)^{-1}$ is still a projection onto $W$, it commutes with every $\rho(h)$, and its kernel is an invariant complement.

blocks.title: Unitarity and the averaging projection
blocks.body:
The proof gives more: in the averaged inner product every $\rho(g)$ preserves lengths, so it is a unitary operator. By [[spectral-theorem|the spectral theorem]] each $\rho(g)$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues of absolute value $1$, and since $\rho(g)^{|G|} = I$ these eigenvalues are roots of unity. Every complex representation of a finite group can be written, in a suitable basis, with unitary matrices.

The same averaging idea gives a formula that is useful by itself. Let $V^G = \{v : \rho(g)v = v \text{ for all } g\}$ be the subspace of fixed vectors, and set
$$P = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \rho(g).$$
For any $h$, $\rho(h)P = P$ (reindex the sum), so every vector $Pv$ is fixed; and if $v$ is fixed then $Pv = v$. Hence $P$ is a projection onto $V^G$, so $P^2 = P$, and the trace of a projection equals its rank:
$$\dim V^G = \operatorname{tr} P = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \operatorname{tr} \rho(g).$$

blocks.title: Example 2: counting orbits with the averaging formula
blocks.body: How many ways are there to colour the $6$ beads of a necklace black or white, if two colourings that differ by a rotation are considered the same?
blocks.solution:
Let $X$ be the set of $2^6 = 64$ colourings, with $G = \mathbb{Z}/6$ acting by rotation, and take the permutation representation $\mathbb{C}^X$. A vector $\sum c_x e_x$ is fixed by $G$ exactly when $c$ is constant on each orbit, so $\dim (\mathbb{C}^X)^G$ is the number of orbits, which is what we want. And $\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$ is the trace of a permutation matrix, which is the number of colourings fixed by $g$. The formula above becomes Burnside's counting lemma: the number of orbits is the average number of fixed points.

A rotation by $k$ steps splits the $6$ positions into $\gcd(k,6)$ cycles, and a colouring is fixed exactly when it is constant on each cycle, so it fixes $2^{\gcd(k,6)}$ colourings. For $k = 0,1,2,3,4,5$ this gives $64, 2, 4, 8, 4, 2$, with sum $84$. The answer is $84/6 = 14$ necklaces.

blocks.title: Schur's lemma
blocks.body:
Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of $G$ and $T\colon V \to W$ a $G$-map.

1. Either $T = 0$ or $T$ is an isomorphism.
2. If $V = W$ is a complex representation, then $T = \lambda I$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$.

1. The kernel of $T$ is invariant: if $Tv = 0$ then $T\rho(g)v = \sigma(g)Tv = 0$. Since $V$ is irreducible, $\ker T$ is $0$ or $V$. Similarly the image of $T$ is an invariant subspace of $W$, so it is $0$ or $W$. If $T \ne 0$ then $\ker T = 0$ and $\operatorname{im} T = W$, so $T$ is an isomorphism.

2. As $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed and $V$ is finite-dimensional, $T$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. Then $T - \lambda I$ is also a $G$-map, and it is not injective. By part 1 it is zero, so $T = \lambda I$.

blocks.title: Abelian groups
blocks.body:
Schur's lemma has an immediate consequence for abelian groups. If $G$ is abelian and $V$ is irreducible, then each $\rho(h)$ commutes with every $\rho(g)$, so $\rho(h)$ is a $G$-map and therefore a scalar. But then every subspace of $V$ is invariant, and irreducibility forces $\dim V = 1$. Every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is $1$-dimensional.

For $G = \mathbb{Z}/n$ this means: a representation is the same as one invertible matrix $A = \rho(1)$ with $A^n = I$, and Maschke's theorem says $A$ can be diagonalised, with eigenvalues among the $n$-th roots of unity. The irreducible representations are the $n$ characters $\rho_j(k) = \omega^{jk}$ for $j = 0, \dots, n-1$, and decomposing a representation of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ into them is the same as the discrete Fourier transform.

The field matters. The rotation representation of $\mathbb{Z}/4$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$ (no real line is fixed by a $90^\circ$ rotation), but over $\mathbb{C}$ it splits, as the next example shows.

blocks.title: Example 3: rotations of the plane over C
blocks.body: Let $\mathbb{Z}/4$ act on $\mathbb{C}^2$ by $\rho(k) = R^k$ with $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ (rotation by $90^\circ$). Decompose it into irreducibles.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $R$ is $\lambda^2 + 1$, with roots $\pm i$. Eigenvectors: $R(1, -i)^{\mathsf T} = (i, 1)^{\mathsf T} = i\,(1,-i)^{\mathsf T}$ and $R(1, i)^{\mathsf T} = (-i, 1)^{\mathsf T} = -i\,(1, i)^{\mathsf T}$. The two eigenlines are invariant under every power of $R$, so
$$\mathbb{C}^2 = \mathbb{C}(1,-i) \oplus \mathbb{C}(1,i) \cong \rho_1 \oplus \rho_3,$$
where $\rho_j(k) = i^{jk}$: on the first line $k$ acts by $i^k$, on the second by $(-i)^k = i^{3k}$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ no such decomposition exists, because $R$ has no real eigenvalue.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
Maschke's theorem says every representation is built from irreducibles; the next questions are how many irreducibles a group has and how big they are. The answers, proved on the page on [[character-theory]], are remarkably rigid. A finite group has only finitely many irreducible representations up to equivalence, say $V_1, \dots, V_k$; their number $k$ equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$; each $V_i$ appears in the regular representation exactly $\dim V_i$ times; and so
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} (\dim V_i)^2 = |G|.$$
For $S_3$ there are three conjugacy classes and three irreducibles: trivial, sign and the $2$-dimensional one of Example 1, and indeed $1 + 1 + 4 = 6$. Moreover the multiplicity of each $V_i$ in any representation is determined, even though the subspaces themselves may not be.

Two further constructions are used constantly. If $V$, $W$ are representations, so are $V \oplus W$, the tensor product $V \otimes W$ with $g$ acting by $\rho(g) \otimes \sigma(g)$ (see [[tensor-products]]), and the dual $V^*$. And a representation of $G$ on $V$ is the same thing as a module over the group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$, so the theory is a chapter of the theory of [[modules]]; in this language Maschke's theorem says that $\mathbb{C}[G]$ is a semisimple ring.

- Maschke's theorem needs a finite group (or, later, a compact one) and a field of characteristic not dividing $|G|$. The two counterexamples above show that neither hypothesis can be dropped.
- The decomposition into irreducibles is unique only up to isomorphism and reordering, not as a set of subspaces. In $\mathbb{C}^2$ with $G$ acting trivially, every line is an invariant subspace, and any two distinct lines give a decomposition.
- An invariant subspace is not the same as a subspace of fixed vectors: the plane $P$ in Example 1 is invariant, yet $S_3$ fixes no nonzero vector in it.
- Equivalent representations can look very different as matrices; to compare them, use a basis-free invariant such as the character.

Characters, the traces of representations, turn all of this into computation; see [[character-theory]]. The irreducible representations of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ are the exponentials of the discrete Fourier transform, and for the circle group the analogous decomposition of functions is the theory of [[fourier-series]]. For compact groups such as rotation groups the average over $G$ is replaced by an integral, and the theory continues on [[lie-groups]] and [[lie-algebras]]. In quantum mechanics, the states of a system with symmetry group $G$ form a representation of $G$, and the decomposition into irreducibles explains the degeneracies of energy levels. Representations are also the functors from a one-object category to vector spaces; see [[categories-functors]].

1. Show that every $1$-dimensional representation of $S_n$ is either trivial or the sign. (Hint: transpositions are all conjugate.)
2. Decompose the permutation representation of $\mathbb{Z}/3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ (cyclic shift of coordinates) into three $1$-dimensional representations, giving an eigenvector for each.
3. Show that the representation of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ on $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ given by $k \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has exactly one invariant line.
4. Use the averaging formula to count the colourings of the four cells of a $2 \times 2$ board with three colours, up to rotation of the board.

Fulton & Harris, Representation Theory: A First Course
James & Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups

entry.sum: The character of a representation $\rho$ is the function $\chi(g) = \operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$, constant on conjugacy classes. For a finite group over $\mathbb{C}$ the irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis of the class functions, so a representation is determined by its character, its decomposition is read off from inner products, and the number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes.
key: \langle \chi, \psi \rangle = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}\chi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}, \qquad \langle \chi_i, \chi_j\rangle = \delta_{ij}
V \cong \bigoplus_i V_i^{\,m_i} \iff m_i = \langle \chi_V, \chi_i \rangle \text{ for all } i
\sum_{i=1}^{k} (\dim V_i)^2 = |G|, \qquad k = \#\{\text{conjugacy classes of } G\}
entry.why: Characters turn questions about matrices into arithmetic with a small square table; they classify representations, prove structural results about groups such as Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem, and in their abelian form (Dirichlet characters) separate primes into arithmetic progressions.

links.note: Dirichlet characters are the characters of the abelian group $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$, and their orthogonality is used to isolate primes in a single residue class in Dirichlet's theorem.
Character tables of point groups are used in quantum mechanics and spectroscopy to classify molecular vibrations and electronic states and to derive selection rules.
Characters give exact formulas for the distribution of random walks generated by conjugacy classes, as in the Diaconis–Shahshahani analysis of random transpositions on $S_n$.

refs: Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups
James & Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups
Isaacs, Character Theory of Finite Groups

blocks.body:
A representation of a finite group is a whole family of matrices, one per group element, and the same representation looks different in every basis. How can we tell whether two representations are equivalent, or find which irreducible pieces a representation contains, without diagonalising anything?

The answer is to keep just one number per group element: the trace. The resulting function on the group, the character, forgets almost everything, yet over $\mathbb{C}$ it determines the representation up to equivalence. Better still, the characters of the irreducible representations are orthonormal for a natural inner product, so decomposing a representation becomes a matter of computing a few inner products, exactly like finding coordinates in an orthonormal basis. This page builds on [[group-representations]] (Maschke's theorem, Schur's lemma and the averaging formula for fixed vectors). All representations are finite-dimensional and complex, and $G$ is a finite group.

blocks.title: Character
blocks.body:
The character of a representation $\rho\colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$ is the function
$$\chi_V\colon G \to \mathbb{C}, \qquad \chi_V(g) = \operatorname{tr} \rho(g).$$
Its degree is $\chi_V(1) = \dim V$. A function $f\colon G \to \mathbb{C}$ that is constant on conjugacy classes, $f(hgh^{-1}) = f(g)$, is a class function. The characters of irreducible representations are called irreducible characters.

So a character is a short list of numbers, one for each conjugacy class (it is a class function, as shown next).

blocks.title: Basic properties
blocks.body:
1. Class function: $\chi(hgh^{-1}) = \operatorname{tr}(\rho(h)\rho(g)\rho(h)^{-1}) = \operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$, since similar matrices have equal trace. Equivalent representations have equal characters for the same reason.
2. Each $\rho(g)$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ that are roots of unity (see [[group-representations]]). So $\chi(g) = \lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n$, hence $|\chi(g)| \le n = \chi(1)$, and since $\lambda^{-1} = \overline{\lambda}$ for $|\lambda| = 1$, we get $\chi(g^{-1}) = \overline{\chi(g)}$.
3. Sums and products: $\chi_{V \oplus W} = \chi_V + \chi_W$, and $\chi_{V \otimes W} = \chi_V \chi_W$ because the eigenvalues of $\rho(g) \otimes \sigma(g)$ are the products $\lambda_i \mu_j$. The dual has $\chi_{V^*} = \overline{\chi_V}$.
4. Permutation representations: if $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, the character of $\mathbb{C}^X$ is $\chi(g) = |\{x : gx = x\}|$, the number of fixed points, since a permutation matrix has trace equal to the number of $1$'s on its diagonal.
5. The regular representation ($G$ acting on itself by left multiplication) has $\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}(1) = |G|$ and $\chi_{\mathrm{reg}}(g) = 0$ for $g \ne 1$, since $gx = x$ forces $g = 1$.

For $S_3$, with conjugacy classes $\{1\}$, the three transpositions, and the two $3$-cycles, the permutation representation on $\mathbb{C}^3$ has character $(3, 1, 0)$ on these classes; the trivial and sign characters are $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,-1,1)$; and the $2$-dimensional representation on the plane $x+y+z = 0$ has character $(3,1,0) - (1,1,1) = (2, 0, -1)$.

blocks.title: Inner product of class functions
blocks.body:
For functions $\varphi, \psi\colon G \to \mathbb{C}$ put
$$\langle \varphi, \psi \rangle = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \varphi(g)\overline{\psi(g)} .$$
This is an inner product on the space of class functions. If $G$ has conjugacy classes $C_1, \dots, C_k$ with representatives $g_1, \dots, g_k$, it can be computed class by class: $\langle \varphi, \psi\rangle = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{j} |C_j|\,\varphi(g_j)\overline{\psi(g_j)}$.

blocks.title: Orthogonality of characters
blocks.body:
For any representations $V$, $W$ of $G$,
$$\dim \mathrm{Hom}_G(V, W) = \langle \chi_W, \chi_V \rangle .$$
In particular, if $V$ and $W$ are irreducible then $\langle \chi_V, \chi_W \rangle = 1$ when $V \cong W$ and $0$ otherwise: the irreducible characters are orthonormal.

The space $H = \mathrm{Hom}(V, W)$ of all linear maps is itself a representation of $G$, with $g$ acting by $A \mapsto \sigma(g) A \rho(g)^{-1}$. A vector $A \in H$ is fixed by every $g$ exactly when $\sigma(g)A = A\rho(g)$ for all $g$, that is, when $A$ is a $G$-map. So $H^G = \mathrm{Hom}_G(V, W)$, and by the averaging formula
$$\dim \mathrm{Hom}_G(V, W) = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g} \chi_H(g).$$
To compute $\chi_H(g)$ fix $g$ and choose bases $e_1, \dots, e_m$ of $V$ and $f_1, \dots, f_n$ of $W$ in which $\rho(g) = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_m)$ and $\sigma(g) = \mathrm{diag}(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_n)$. The maps $E_{ji}$ sending $e_i$ to $f_j$ and the other $e$'s to $0$ form a basis of $H$, and
$$\sigma(g) E_{ji}\rho(g)^{-1} = \mu_j \lambda_i^{-1} E_{ji}.$$
So the action of $g$ on $H$ is diagonal in this basis, and its trace is $\sum_{i,j} \mu_j \lambda_i^{-1} = \big(\sum_j \mu_j\big)\big(\sum_i \overline{\lambda_i}\big) = \chi_W(g)\overline{\chi_V(g)}$. Substituting gives the formula.

If $V$ and $W$ are irreducible, Schur's lemma says $\mathrm{Hom}_G(V,W) = 0$ when $V \not\cong W$, and when $V \cong W$ it is identified with $\mathrm{End}_G(V)$, the scalars, of dimension $1$. Since these numbers are real, $\langle \chi_W, \chi_V\rangle = \overline{\langle \chi_V, \chi_W\rangle} = \langle \chi_V, \chi_W\rangle$.

blocks.title: Consequences: multiplicities and the regular representation
blocks.body:
Let $V_1, \dots, V_k$ be the irreducible representations up to equivalence, with characters $\chi_1, \dots, \chi_k$ and degrees $d_i = \chi_i(1)$. (There are finitely many, because orthonormal vectors in a finite-dimensional space are linearly independent.) By Maschke's theorem any representation is $V \cong V_1^{m_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_k^{m_k}$, so $\chi_V = \sum m_i \chi_i$, and taking inner products:

1. Multiplicities: $m_i = \langle \chi_V, \chi_i \rangle$. Hence the character determines the multiplicities, and so determines $V$ up to equivalence.
2. Irreducibility test: $\langle \chi_V, \chi_V \rangle = \sum m_i^2$, which equals $1$ exactly when $V$ is irreducible.
3. The regular representation: $m_i = \langle \chi_{\mathrm{reg}}, \chi_i \rangle = \frac{1}{|G|}\,|G|\,\overline{\chi_i(1)} = d_i$. Every irreducible occurs in the regular representation, $d_i$ times, and comparing dimensions,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} d_i^2 = |G|.$$

For the $S_3$ characters above (class sizes $1, 3, 2$): $\langle (2,0,-1), (2,0,-1)\rangle = (4 + 0 + 2)/6 = 1$, confirming irreducibility, and the permutation character decomposes as $\langle (3,1,0), \text{triv}\rangle = (3+3+0)/6 = 1$, $\langle (3,1,0), \text{sign}\rangle = (3-3+0)/6 = 0$, $\langle (3,1,0), (2,0,-1)\rangle = (6+0+0)/6 = 1$, matching $\mathbb{C}^3 = \text{triv} \oplus \text{standard}$.

blocks.title: Characters span the class functions
blocks.body: The irreducible characters $\chi_1, \dots, \chi_k$ form an orthonormal basis of the space of class functions on $G$. Consequently the number of irreducible representations of $G$ equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$.

They are orthonormal, so it remains to show that a class function $f$ with $\langle \chi_i, f \rangle = 0$ for all $i$ is zero. For any representation $(\rho, V)$ consider $T = \sum_{g} \overline{f(g)}\,\rho(g)$. It is a $G$-map: substituting $g' = hgh^{-1}$ and using $f(h^{-1}g'h) = f(g')$,
$$\rho(h) T \rho(h)^{-1} = \sum_g \overline{f(g)}\rho(hgh^{-1}) = \sum_{g'} \overline{f(g')}\rho(g') = T.$$
On an irreducible $V_i$, Schur's lemma makes $T$ a scalar $\lambda$, and taking traces, $\lambda d_i = \sum_g \overline{f(g)}\chi_i(g) = |G|\langle \chi_i, f\rangle = 0$. So $T = 0$ on every irreducible, hence on every representation by Maschke's theorem, in particular on the regular representation. There $T$ applied to the basis vector $e_1$ gives $\sum_g \overline{f(g)} e_g = 0$, so $f(g) = 0$ for every $g$.

The space of class functions has dimension $k'$, the number of conjugacy classes (a basis is given by the indicator functions of the classes), so $k = k'$.

blocks.title: The character table and column orthogonality
blocks.body:
The character table of $G$ lists the irreducible characters as rows and the conjugacy classes as columns; by the theorem it is square. Row orthogonality is the theorem above. Columns are orthogonal too: for $g, h \in G$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} \chi_i(g)\overline{\chi_i(h)} = \begin{cases} |C_G(g)| & \text{if } g, h \text{ are conjugate},\\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}$$
where $C_G(g)$ is the centraliser. Proof: the $k \times k$ matrix with entries $u_{ij} = \sqrt{|C_j|/|G|}\,\chi_i(g_j)$ has orthonormal rows, so it is unitary, so its columns are orthonormal as well; this is the displayed formula after using $|G|/|C_j| = |C_G(g_j)|$ (orbit–stabiliser for conjugation). The column through $g = h = 1$ recovers $\sum d_i^2 = |G|$.

Some deeper facts, stated without proof: character values are algebraic integers; each degree $d_i$ divides $|G|$; and characters are the main tool in Burnside's theorem that a group of order $p^a q^b$ is solvable (see [[solvable-groups]]).

blocks.title: Example 1: a tensor square
blocks.body: Decompose $V \otimes V$, where $V$ is the $2$-dimensional irreducible representation of $S_3$.
blocks.solution:
Characters multiply, so on the classes (identity, transpositions, $3$-cycles), with sizes $1, 3, 2$, the character of $V \otimes V$ is $(2,0,-1)^2 = (4, 0, 1)$. Then
$$\langle (4,0,1), \text{triv}\rangle = \tfrac{4 + 0 + 2}{6} = 1,\quad \langle (4,0,1), \text{sign}\rangle = \tfrac{4 - 0 + 2}{6} = 1,\quad \langle (4,0,1), (2,0,-1)\rangle = \tfrac{8 + 0 - 2}{6} = 1.$$
So $V \otimes V \cong \text{triv} \oplus \text{sign} \oplus V$; dimensions agree, $4 = 1 + 1 + 2$. No basis or matrix was needed.

blocks.title: Example 2: building a character table
blocks.body: Find the character table of the dihedral group $D_4 = \langle r, s \mid r^4 = s^2 = 1,\ srs^{-1} = r^{-1}\rangle$ of order $8$, the symmetry group of a square.
blocks.solution:
Conjugacy classes. Conjugating by $s$ inverts $r$, and $r$ conjugates $s$ to $sr^{-2}$; one finds the five classes
$$\{1\},\ \{r^2\},\ \{r, r^3\},\ \{s, sr^2\},\ \{sr, sr^3\},$$
with sizes $1,1,2,2,2$. So there are five irreducible characters, with $\sum d_i^2 = 8$.

Degree-$1$ characters. A homomorphism $\chi\colon D_4 \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ is determined by $\chi(r), \chi(s)$. From $s^2 = 1$ we get $\chi(s) = \pm 1$, and from $srs^{-1} = r^{-1}$ we get $\chi(r) = \chi(r)^{-1}$, so $\chi(r) = \pm 1$; all four sign choices are consistent with the relations. That gives four linear characters, and $8 = 4\cdot 1 + d^2$ forces one more irreducible of degree $d = 2$.

The last row. Column orthogonality between the column of $1$ and each other column says $\sum_i \chi_i(1)\chi_i(g) = 0$ for $g \ne 1$. On the classes in the order above the table is
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} & 1 & r^2 & r & s & sr \\ \hline \chi_1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\ \chi_2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & -1 & -1 \\ \chi_3 & 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ \chi_4 & 1 & 1 & -1 & -1 & 1 \\ \chi_5 & 2 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}$$
where the last row comes from, e.g., $1+1+1+1 + 2\chi_5(r^2) = 0$ and $1 + 1 - 1 - 1 + 2\chi_5(r) = 0$. As a check, $\chi_5$ is the character of $D_4$ acting on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by its symmetries of the square: rotation by $180^\circ$ has trace $-2$, rotation by $90^\circ$ and every reflection have trace $0$.

The quaternion group $Q_8 = \{\pm 1, \pm i, \pm j, \pm k\}$ has exactly the same table (classes $\{1\}, \{-1\}, \{\pm i\}, \{\pm j\}, \{\pm k\}$), although it is not isomorphic to $D_4$: $D_4$ has five elements of order $2$ and $Q_8$ has one.

blocks.title: Example 3: how commutative can a non-abelian group be?
blocks.body: The probability that two independently and uniformly chosen elements of $G$ commute is $k/|G|$, where $k$ is the number of conjugacy classes. Prove this, and use characters to show that for a non-abelian group this probability is at most $5/8$.
blocks.solution:
Counting. For fixed $g$, the elements commuting with $g$ form the centraliser $C_G(g)$, and by orbit–stabiliser $|C_G(g)| = |G|/|\mathrm{cl}(g)|$. So the number of commuting pairs is
$$\sum_{g} |C_G(g)| = |G| \sum_{g} \frac{1}{|\mathrm{cl}(g)|} = |G| \cdot k,$$
since each class contributes $|\mathrm{cl}(g)| \cdot \frac{1}{|\mathrm{cl}(g)|} = 1$. Dividing by $|G|^2$ gives $k/|G|$.

The bound. Let $L$ be the number of degree-$1$ characters. They are the homomorphisms $G \to \mathbb{C}^\times$, and since $\mathbb{C}^\times$ is abelian they all factor through the abelianisation $G/G'$ (where $G'$ is the commutator subgroup); conversely each degree-$1$ character of $G/G'$ gives one of $G$. An abelian group has all irreducible degrees equal to $1$ (Schur), so by $\sum d_i^2 = |G/G'|$ it has exactly $|G/G'|$ of them. Thus $L = |G/G'|$. If $G$ is non-abelian then $G' \ne 1$ and $L \le |G|/2$.

Every other irreducible has degree at least $2$, so
$$|G| = \sum_i d_i^2 \ge L + 4(k - L) = 4k - 3L \ge 4k - \tfrac{3}{2}|G|.$$
Hence $k \le \tfrac{5}{8}|G|$, and the probability is at most $5/8$. Equality holds for $D_4$: $k = 5$, $|G| = 8$.

blocks.body:
- A character is not a homomorphism unless it has degree $1$: for $D_4$, $\chi_5(r)^2 = 0$ but $\chi_5(r^2) = -2$.
- The inner product needs the complex conjugate. For groups with non-real character values (cyclic groups of order at least $3$, $A_4$) forgetting it gives wrong multiplicities.
- Characters determine representations, but the character table does not determine the group: $D_4$ and $Q_8$ share a table.
- Everything here is over $\mathbb{C}$ (or characteristic $0$). In characteristic $p$ dividing $|G|$, traces no longer determine representations and the theory of modular characters is different.
- When computing $\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle$ class by class, remember the class sizes; the sum is over group elements, not over classes.

For an abelian group, the irreducible characters are homomorphisms to $\mathbb{C}^\times$, and orthogonality is the engine of discrete Fourier analysis. The Dirichlet characters used to count primes in arithmetic progressions are exactly the characters of $(\mathbb{Z}/n)^\times$; see [[dirichlet-characters]], [[gauss-sums]] and [[l-functions]], where orthogonality isolates one residue class. The Legendre symbol of [[quadratic-residues]] is a degree-$1$ character of $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$. Characters of compact groups such as the rotation groups continue the story on [[lie-groups]], and the counting in Example 3 is related to the class equation of [[group-actions]].

1. Write down the character table of $\mathbb{Z}/4$ and of $\mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$, and check that the two tables are different even though both groups have order $4$.
2. Let $S_4$ act on $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Show that $\chi(g) = (\text{number of fixed points of } g) - 1$ is an irreducible character, using $\langle \chi, \chi\rangle = 1$.
3. Prove that if every irreducible character of $G$ has degree $1$, then $G$ is abelian.
4. For a representation $V$ with character $\chi$, show that $\rho(g) = I$ exactly when $\chi(g) = \chi(1)$.

entry.sum: A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with smooth multiplication and inversion. The central examples are matrix groups such as $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ and $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$, which are closed subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ and hence submanifolds; because left translations move the identity to any point, the whole group is governed by its structure near the identity.
key: \mu\colon G \times G \to G,\ (g,h) \mapsto gh \quad\text{and}\quad \iota\colon g \mapsto g^{-1} \text{ are smooth}
\mathrm{SO}(n) = \{A \in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R}) : A^{\mathsf T}A = I,\ \det A = 1\}, \qquad \dim \mathrm{SO}(n) = \tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}
\mathrm{SU}(2) \cong S^3, \qquad \mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\}
entry.why: Lie groups are the continuous symmetry groups of geometry and physics: rotations, the Lorentz group of relativity and the gauge groups of particle physics, and through Noether's theorem each such symmetry gives a conserved quantity.

links.note: Lie groups give basic examples of manifolds with computable topology, such as $\mathrm{SU}(2) \cong S^3$ and $\mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathbb{RP}^3$, whose fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}/2$ is detected by the double cover.
Single-qubit gates are elements of $\mathrm{U}(2)$ (up to phase, $\mathrm{SU}(2)$), and universality of a gate set means that the group it generates is dense in $\mathrm{SU}(2^n)$.
Lie originally introduced continuous groups to study symmetries of differential equations, and symmetry groups are still used to reduce the order of ODEs and to find invariant solutions of PDEs.
