Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations
Stillwell, Naive Lie Theory

blocks.body:
The rotations of three-dimensional space form a group: composing two rotations gives a rotation, and every rotation can be undone. But this group is not a list of elements like a finite group. A rotation is described by an axis and an angle, three real parameters in all, and nearby rotations differ only slightly. The group is at the same time a smooth three-dimensional space on which one can do calculus.

Sophus Lie's idea, in the 1870s, was to study such continuous groups of symmetries through their infinitesimal versions, much as calculus studies a curve through its tangent lines. A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold, with the group operations smooth. Most examples are groups of matrices cut out by polynomial equations: rotation groups, unitary groups, the groups of matrices with determinant $1$. They are the symmetry groups of geometry and of physics. This page assumes [[groups]] and [[smooth-manifolds]] (charts, smooth maps, tangent spaces and the regular value theorem).

blocks.title: Lie group
blocks.body:
A Lie group is a group $G$ that is also a smooth manifold, such that multiplication $G \times G \to G$, $(g,h) \mapsto gh$, and inversion $G \to G$, $g \mapsto g^{-1}$, are smooth maps. A Lie group homomorphism is a group homomorphism that is also a smooth map. The dimension of $G$ is its dimension as a manifold.

So a Lie group is a group in which one can differentiate, and the algebra and the geometry are compatible.

blocks.title: Examples, and matrix groups
blocks.body:
Simple examples: $(\mathbb{R}^n, +)$; the circle $S^1 = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1\}$ under multiplication; the torus $S^1 \times S^1$; any finite or countable group with the discrete topology (a $0$-dimensional Lie group).

The main family consists of matrix groups. The general linear group $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ of invertible real $n \times n$ matrices is an open subset of the space $M_n(\mathbb{R}) \cong \mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ (it is where $\det \ne 0$), hence a manifold of dimension $n^2$. Matrix multiplication is polynomial in the entries and inversion is rational (Cramer's rule), so both are smooth. Inside it sit
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R}) &= \{A : \det A = 1\}, \\
\mathrm{O}(n) &= \{A : A^{\mathsf T}A = I\} \quad \text{(maps preserving lengths)}, \\
\mathrm{SO}(n) &= \{A \in \mathrm{O}(n) : \det A = 1\} \quad \text{(rotations)},
\end{aligned}$$
and, with complex entries and conjugate transpose $A^*$, the unitary groups $\mathrm{U}(n) = \{A : A^*A = I\}$ and $\mathrm{SU}(n) = \{A \in \mathrm{U}(n) : \det A = 1\}$. Each is a subgroup defined by polynomial equations in the entries (real and imaginary parts, in the complex case), so it is a closed subset. The next theorem shows these are submanifolds, and computes their dimensions.

blocks.title: Orthogonal and special linear groups are Lie groups
blocks.body:
$\mathrm{O}(n)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ of dimension $n(n-1)/2$, with tangent space at the identity
$$T_I\,\mathrm{O}(n) = \{X \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) : X^{\mathsf T} + X = 0\}.$$
$\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $n^2 - 1$ with $T_I\,\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R}) = \{X : \operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$. Both are Lie groups. Similarly $\dim \mathrm{SO}(n) = n(n-1)/2$, $\dim \mathrm{U}(n) = n^2$ and $\dim \mathrm{SU}(n) = n^2 - 1$.

Let $\mathrm{Sym}_n$ be the space of symmetric matrices, of dimension $n(n+1)/2$, and define $F\colon M_n(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathrm{Sym}_n$ by $F(A) = A^{\mathsf T}A$. Then $\mathrm{O}(n) = F^{-1}(I)$. Expanding $F(A + tX) = A^{\mathsf T}A + t(X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X) + t^2 X^{\mathsf T}X$ shows
$$dF_A(X) = X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X.$$
For $A \in \mathrm{O}(n)$ this is onto $\mathrm{Sym}_n$: given symmetric $S$, put $X = \tfrac12 AS$; then $X^{\mathsf T}A + A^{\mathsf T}X = \tfrac12 S A^{\mathsf T}A + \tfrac12 A^{\mathsf T}AS = S$. So $I$ is a regular value, and by the regular value theorem $\mathrm{O}(n)$ is an embedded submanifold of dimension $n^2 - n(n+1)/2 = n(n-1)/2$, whose tangent space at $I$ is $\ker dF_I = \{X : X^{\mathsf T} + X = 0\}$.

For $\mathrm{SL}_n$, use $\det\colon M_n(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathbb{R}$. For invertible $A$, $\det(A + tX) = \det A \det(I + tA^{-1}X) = \det A\,(1 + t\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}X) + O(t^2))$, so $d(\det)_A(X) = \det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}X)$, which is onto $\mathbb{R}$ (take $X = cA$). Hence $1$ is a regular value, $\dim \mathrm{SL}_n = n^2 - 1$, and $T_I\,\mathrm{SL}_n = \{\operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$.

In each case the group operations are restrictions of the smooth operations of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ to an embedded submanifold, so they are smooth. $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ is the open and closed subset of $\mathrm{O}(n)$ where $\det = +1$ (the determinant of an orthogonal matrix is $\pm 1$), so it has the same dimension. For $\mathrm{U}(n)$ the same argument with Hermitian matrices (real dimension $n^2$) inside $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ (real dimension $2n^2$) gives $\dim \mathrm{U}(n) = n^2$, and $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ is cut out of it by one more real equation.

blocks.title: Closed subgroups and homogeneity
blocks.body:
More generally, Cartan's closed subgroup theorem (stated here without proof) says that every closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded submanifold, hence itself a Lie group. So any closed subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ or $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is a Lie group; these are the matrix Lie groups. The proof uses the exponential map of the next page, [[lie-algebras]].

Two features make Lie groups far more rigid than general manifolds. First, for each $g$ the left translation $L_g(h) = gh$ is a diffeomorphism of $G$ (with inverse $L_{g^{-1}}$) carrying the identity $e$ to $g$. So a Lie group looks the same near every point, and all of its local structure is visible at $e$. In particular its tangent space $\mathfrak{g} = T_eG$ determines a great deal; equipped with a bracket coming from the group law, it is the Lie algebra of $G$. Second, connectivity spreads local information everywhere, as the next theorem shows.

blocks.title: A connected group is generated by any neighbourhood of the identity
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a connected Lie group (more generally, a connected topological group) and $U$ any neighbourhood of the identity. Then every element of $G$ is a finite product of elements of $U$.

Choose an open set $W$ with $e \in W \subseteq U$ and let $V = W \cap W^{-1}$, an open set containing $e$ with $V^{-1} = V$ and $V \subseteq U$, and let $H = \bigcup_{n \ge 1} V^n$, where $V^n$ is the set of products of $n$ elements of $V$. Then $H$ is a subgroup: it is closed under products, and under inverses because $(v_1\cdots v_n)^{-1} = v_n^{-1}\cdots v_1^{-1}$ with each $v_i^{-1} \in V$.

$H$ is open: for $h \in H$, the set $hV$ is open (left translation is a homeomorphism), contains $h$, and lies in $H$. Its complement is open too, being the union of the cosets $gH$ with $g \notin H$, each open for the same reason. So $H$ is nonempty, open and closed, and connectedness of $G$ gives $H = G$.

blocks.title: Example 1: the circle group
blocks.body:
Show that $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ consists exactly of the rotation matrices
$$R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix},$$
that $\theta \mapsto R_\theta$ is a Lie group homomorphism $(\mathbb{R}, +) \to \mathrm{SO}(2)$ with kernel $2\pi\mathbb{Z}$, and that $\mathrm{SO}(2) \cong \mathrm{U}(1) = S^1$.
blocks.solution:
Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}$ with $A^{\mathsf T}A = I$ and $\det A = 1$. The columns are orthonormal, so $(a, c)$ is a unit vector, $(a,c) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ for some $\theta$. The second column is a unit vector orthogonal to the first, so $(b, d) = \pm(-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$, and $\det A = \pm(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = \pm 1$ forces the $+$ sign. So $A = R_\theta$; conversely every $R_\theta$ is in $\mathrm{SO}(2)$.

The addition formulas for sine and cosine are precisely the statement $R_\theta R_\varphi = R_{\theta + \varphi}$, so $\theta \mapsto R_\theta$ is a homomorphism; it is smooth, and $R_\theta = I$ exactly when $\theta \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$. Finally $R_\theta \mapsto e^{i\theta}$ is a well-defined bijective homomorphism onto $\mathrm{U}(1) = \{z : |z| = 1\}$ (it is multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ on $\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}^2$), smooth with smooth inverse. All three groups are the circle.

blocks.title: Example 2: SU(2) is a 3-sphere and covers SO(3) twice
blocks.body:
Show that
$$\mathrm{SU}(2) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & -\overline{b} \\ b & \overline{a} \end{pmatrix} : a, b \in \mathbb{C},\ |a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1 \right\},$$
so that $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is diffeomorphic to the $3$-sphere $S^3 \subset \mathbb{C}^2 = \mathbb{R}^4$. Then describe the homomorphism $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathrm{SO}(3)$ and its kernel.
blocks.solution:
The form. A unitary matrix has orthonormal columns. If the first column is $(a, b)$ with $|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1$, the second column is a unit vector orthogonal to it, so it is $\lambda(-\overline{b}, \overline{a})$ with $|\lambda| = 1$ (the orthogonal complement of $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is the line through $(-\overline{b}, \overline{a})$). The determinant is $\lambda(|a|^2 + |b|^2) = \lambda$, so $\det = 1$ forces $\lambda = 1$. Conversely every such matrix is unitary with determinant $1$. The map to $(a, b) \in S^3$ is a diffeomorphism. In particular $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is connected and simply connected.

The covering of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the real $3$-dimensional space of traceless Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices
$$X = \begin{pmatrix} z & x - iy \\ x + iy & -z \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det X = -(x^2 + y^2 + z^2).$$
For $U \in \mathrm{SU}(2)$ the map $X \mapsto UXU^{-1}$ preserves $\mathcal{H}$ and preserves the determinant, so it is a linear map of $\mathbb{R}^3$ preserving $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$, an element of $\mathrm{O}(3)$. This gives a smooth homomorphism $\Phi\colon \mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathrm{O}(3)$; as $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is connected and $\det \Phi(U) = \pm 1$ varies continuously, the image lies in $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. The kernel consists of the $U$ commuting with every element of $\mathcal{H}$, hence (since $\mathcal{H}$ together with $I$ spans all complex $2 \times 2$ matrices) with every matrix, so $U$ is a scalar of determinant $1$: $U = \pm I$. One can show (we omit the proof) that $\Phi$ is onto, so
$$\mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\} \cong S^3/(\text{antipodal map}) = \mathbb{RP}^3 .$$
Topologically, $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is not simply connected: its [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] is $\mathbb{Z}/2$. This is the mathematics behind spin in quantum mechanics.

blocks.title: Example 3: every rotation of space has an axis
blocks.body: (Euler's rotation theorem.) Prove that every $A \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ has a fixed axis: there is a unit vector $v$ with $Av = v$.
blocks.solution:
We show $\det(A - I) = 0$. Using $A A^{\mathsf T} = I$,
$$\det(A - I) = \det(A - AA^{\mathsf T}) = \det A \cdot \det(I - A^{\mathsf T}) = \det\big((I - A)^{\mathsf T}\big) = \det(I - A).$$
For $3 \times 3$ matrices $\det(I - A) = (-1)^3\det(A - I)$. So $\det(A - I) = -\det(A - I)$, hence $\det(A-I) = 0$, and $1$ is an eigenvalue: some unit vector $v$ satisfies $Av = v$. The plane $v^\perp$ is mapped to itself, and $A$ acts on it by an element of $\mathrm{SO}(2)$, a rotation by some angle (Example 1). So every element of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a rotation about an axis, which confirms the count of three parameters: two for the axis direction and one for the angle.

The same argument works in every odd dimension; in even dimensions it fails, e.g. $-I \in \mathrm{SO}(2)$ fixes no nonzero vector.

blocks.title: Topology, compactness, and where Lie groups appear
blocks.body:
Connected components. $\mathrm{O}(n)$ has two components, $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ and the reflections with $\det = -1$; $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ also has two, according to the sign of the determinant; $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathrm{SL}_n$, $\mathrm{SO}(n)$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ are connected.

Compactness. $\mathrm{O}(n)$, $\mathrm{U}(n)$ and their closed subgroups are compact (closed and bounded in $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ or $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, since every column is a unit vector). The rest of this section states standard theorems without proof. A compact Lie group carries a Haar measure, an invariant probability measure, so one can average over it exactly as one averages over a finite group. Consequently Maschke's theorem from [[group-representations]] holds for continuous finite-dimensional representations of compact groups, and the Peter–Weyl theorem extends Fourier series from the circle to every compact Lie group.

Rigidity. A continuous homomorphism between Lie groups is automatically smooth, and the solution of Hilbert's fifth problem (Gleason, Montgomery and Zippin, 1952) shows that every topological group that is locally Euclidean admits a Lie group structure. Smoothness is forced by the group structure.

Physics. $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is the symmetry group of a rotationally invariant system, and by Noether's theorem this symmetry corresponds to conservation of angular momentum. The Lorentz group $\mathrm{O}(1,3)$ of matrices preserving $t^2 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2$ is the symmetry group of special relativity, and the gauge group of the Standard Model is $\mathrm{SU}(3) \times \mathrm{SU}(2) \times \mathrm{U}(1)$.

- Not every Lie group is a matrix group: the universal cover of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ has no faithful finite-dimensional representation. Matrix groups are the main examples, not the definition.
- A subgroup that is a nice curve need not be a Lie subgroup in the embedded sense. In the torus $S^1 \times S^1$ the subgroup $\{(e^{it}, e^{iat}) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ with $a$ irrational is dense, not closed, and not an embedded submanifold.
- Count real dimensions: $\mathrm{U}(n)$ consists of complex matrices but has real dimension $n^2$; it is not a complex submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb{C})$.
- $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ look the same near the identity (both are $3$-dimensional with the same tangent structure) but are not isomorphic: one is simply connected, the other has fundamental group $\mathbb{Z}/2$.

The tangent space at the identity, with the bracket inherited from the group law, is the subject of [[lie-algebras]], where the exponential map $X \mapsto e^X$ connects it back to the group. Representations of compact Lie groups extend [[group-representations]] and [[character-theory]], and for the circle they reduce to [[fourier-series]]. Lie groups acting on manifolds give the homogeneous spaces of [[riemannian-geometry]], such as spheres $S^{n-1} = \mathrm{SO}(n)/\mathrm{SO}(n-1)$, and their topology is studied with [[fundamental-group]] and [[homology]]. The underlying point-set notions are on [[topological-spaces]].

1. The symplectic group $\mathrm{Sp}(2n, \mathbb{R}) = \{A : A^{\mathsf T}JA = J\}$, where $J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_n \\ -I_n & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, is a Lie group. Imitate the proof for $\mathrm{O}(n)$ to show that its dimension is $n(2n+1)$.
2. Show that $\det\colon \mathrm{U}(n) \to \mathrm{U}(1)$ is a surjective Lie group homomorphism with kernel $\mathrm{SU}(n)$, and deduce $\dim \mathrm{SU}(n) = n^2 - 1$ again.
3. Show that $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is not compact, and that $\mathrm{O}(n)$ is compact.
4. Find an element of $\mathrm{SO}(4)$ that fixes no nonzero vector of $\mathbb{R}^4$.

entry.sum: A Lie algebra is a vector space with a bilinear, antisymmetric bracket $[X,Y]$ satisfying the Jacobi identity. The tangent space at the identity of a Lie group is a Lie algebra, with $[X,Y] = XY - YX$ for matrix groups, and the exponential map $X \mapsto e^X$ carries it back to the group. The idea to remember: the bracket records, to second order, how far the group is from commutative, and this is enough to recover the group near the identity.
key: e^{X} = \sum_{k \ge 0} \frac{X^k}{k!}, \qquad \det e^{X} = e^{\operatorname{tr} X}
e^{tX}e^{tY}e^{-tX}e^{-tY} = I + t^2[X,Y] + O(t^3)
entry.why: It linearises continuous symmetry: questions about Lie groups and their representations reduce to linear algebra, as in the classification of simple Lie algebras and in quantum mechanics, where the commutation relations of angular momentum are the bracket of $\mathfrak{so}(3)$.

links.note: Vector fields on any manifold form an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra under the Lie bracket, and the Lie algebra of a Lie group is identified with its left-invariant vector fields.
The solution of the linear system $x' = Ax$ is $x(t) = e^{tA}x(0)$, and Lie algebras of symmetry generators are used to integrate and reduce nonlinear ODEs.

A Hamiltonian $H$ generates the gates $e^{-itH}$, and a set of Hamiltonians $H_k$ allows every gate up to phase when the Lie algebra generated by the skew-Hermitian matrices $iH_k$ contains $\mathfrak{su}(2^n)$.

blocks.body:
A Lie group such as the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a curved space, and its multiplication is a complicated nonlinear map. Near the identity, though, it looks like its tangent space, a plain vector space: an infinitesimal rotation is just an angular velocity vector. Can the whole group be understood from this linear object?

Almost. The tangent space $\mathfrak{g}$ alone has lost the information that the group is not commutative, but that information survives in one extra operation, the bracket $[X, Y]$, which measures to second order how much $g$ and $h$ fail to commute. A vector space with such a bracket is a Lie algebra, and the exponential map $X \mapsto e^X$ carries it back to the group. Problems about Lie groups then become problems of linear algebra. This page continues [[lie-groups]] and works mostly with matrix groups, where everything can be computed by hand.

blocks.title: The matrix exponential
blocks.body:
For a real or complex $n \times n$ matrix $X$ define
$$e^X = \exp(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{X^k}{k!} = I + X + \frac{X^2}{2} + \frac{X^3}{6} + \cdots .$$
The series converges absolutely for every $X$, because $\|X^k\| \le \|X\|^k$ for the operator norm and $\sum \|X\|^k/k!$ converges. Its basic properties, all proved like the corresponding facts for the real exponential:

1. If $XY = YX$ then $e^{X+Y} = e^X e^Y$ (multiply the series and use the binomial theorem, which is valid for commuting matrices). In particular $e^{(s+t)X} = e^{sX}e^{tX}$, and $e^X$ is invertible with inverse $e^{-X}$.
2. $\frac{d}{dt} e^{tX} = X e^{tX} = e^{tX}X$ (differentiate the series term by term), so $x(t) = e^{tX}x_0$ solves the linear system $x' = Xx$, $x(0) = x_0$.
3. $e^{AXA^{-1}} = A e^X A^{-1}$ for invertible $A$, since $(AXA^{-1})^k = AX^kA^{-1}$.
4. $\det e^X = e^{\operatorname{tr} X}$.

Property 1 says that $t \mapsto e^{tX}$ is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb{R}, +)$ into $\mathrm{GL}_n$, a one-parameter subgroup, whose velocity at $t = 0$ is $X$. For example, with
$$J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad J^2 = -I, \quad e^{tJ} = \cos t \, I + \sin t \, J = \begin{pmatrix} \cos t & -\sin t \\ \sin t & \cos t \end{pmatrix},$$
by splitting the series into even and odd powers. The infinitesimal rotation $J$ generates the circle of rotations.

Proof of property 4. Let $f(t) = \det e^{tX}$. Using $d(\det)_A(Y) = \det(A)\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}Y)$ (proved on [[lie-groups]]) and property 2,
$$f'(t) = \det(e^{tX})\operatorname{tr}\big(e^{-tX} X e^{tX}\big) = f(t)\operatorname{tr} X.$$
With $f(0) = 1$ this gives $f(t) = e^{t \operatorname{tr} X}$; put $t = 1$.

blocks.title: Lie algebra of a matrix group
blocks.body:
Let $G \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ or $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a closed subgroup. Its Lie algebra is
$$\mathfrak{g} = \{X \in M_n : e^{tX} \in G \text{ for all } t \in \mathbb{R}\}.$$
One proves (we omit the proof; see Hall) that $\mathfrak{g}$ is a real vector space and equals the tangent space $T_I G$; the exponential map $\exp\colon \mathfrak{g} \to G$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of $0$ onto a neighbourhood of $I$ (its differential at $0$ is the identity).

So $\mathfrak{g}$ is the set of velocities of one-parameter subgroups of $G$.

blocks.title: The classical examples
blocks.body:
The definition makes the standard Lie algebras easy to compute.

- $\mathfrak{gl}_n$: all matrices, since $e^{tX}$ is always invertible.
- $\mathfrak{sl}_n = \{X : \operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$. By property 4, $\det e^{tX} = e^{t \operatorname{tr} X}$, and this equals $1$ for all $t$ exactly when $\operatorname{tr} X = 0$.
- $\mathfrak{so}(n) = \{X \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) : X^{\mathsf T} = -X\}$. If $X^{\mathsf T} = -X$, then $X^{\mathsf T}$ commutes with $X$ and $(e^{tX})^{\mathsf T}e^{tX} = e^{-tX}e^{tX} = I$; also $\det e^{tX} = e^{0} = 1$, so $e^{tX} \in \mathrm{SO}(n)$. Conversely, differentiating $(e^{tX})^{\mathsf T} e^{tX} = I$ at $t = 0$ gives $X^{\mathsf T} + X = 0$.
- $\mathfrak{u}(n) = \{X : X^* = -X\}$ (skew-Hermitian), and $\mathfrak{su}(n) = \{X : X^* = -X,\ \operatorname{tr} X = 0\}$, by the same arguments.

The dimensions agree with those of the groups found on [[lie-groups]]: $n(n-1)/2$ for $\mathfrak{so}(n)$, $n^2 - 1$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb{R})$, $n^2$ for $\mathfrak{u}(n)$.

blocks.title: Where the bracket comes from
blocks.body:
The tangent space is a vector space, but the group is not commutative, and the trace this leaves on $\mathfrak{g}$ is the commutator of matrices
$$[X, Y] = XY - YX.$$
Two ways to see it appear:

The group commutator. Expanding each factor to second order,
$$e^{tX}e^{tY}e^{-tX}e^{-tY} = I + t^2 [X, Y] + O(t^3).$$
(The first-order terms cancel; at second order the squares $X^2, Y^2$ cancel against cross terms, leaving $XY - YX$.) So $[X,Y]$ is the leading term of the failure of $e^{tX}$ and $e^{tY}$ to commute. If $G$ is commutative, the bracket is zero.

Conjugation. For $X, Y \in \mathfrak{g}$ and each $t$, the matrix $e^{tX}Ye^{-tX}$ lies in $\mathfrak{g}$, because by property 3 its exponentials $e^{tX}e^{sY}e^{-tX}$ lie in $G$. Since $\mathfrak{g}$ is a (closed) linear subspace, the derivative at $t = 0$, which is a limit of difference quotients in $\mathfrak{g}$, also lies in $\mathfrak{g}$:
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} e^{tX}Ye^{-tX} = XY - YX = [X, Y].$$
So the Lie algebra of a matrix group is closed under the bracket. This motivates the abstract definition.

blocks.title: Lie algebra
blocks.body:
A Lie algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is a vector space $\mathfrak{g}$ with a bilinear map $[\cdot,\cdot]\colon \mathfrak{g} \times \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{g}$ such that for all $X, Y, Z$
$$[X, X] = 0 \quad (\text{hence } [X,Y] = -[Y,X]), \qquad [X, [Y, Z]] + [Y, [Z, X]] + [Z, [X, Y]] = 0 .$$
The second identity is the Jacobi identity. A homomorphism of Lie algebras is a linear map with $\varphi([X,Y]) = [\varphi(X), \varphi(Y)]$; an ideal is a subspace $\mathfrak{a}$ with $[\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{a}] \subseteq \mathfrak{a}$.

The bracket is not associative; the Jacobi identity is what replaces associativity.

blocks.title: The commutator is a Lie bracket
blocks.body: For matrices (more generally, for elements of any associative algebra) the commutator $[X,Y] = XY - YX$ is bilinear, satisfies $[X,X] = 0$, and satisfies the Jacobi identity. Hence every matrix Lie algebra, with the commutator, is a Lie algebra.

Bilinearity and $[X,X] = XX - XX = 0$ are clear. For Jacobi, expand:
$$[X,[Y,Z]] = XYZ - XZY - YZX + ZYX .$$
Cycling $X \to Y \to Z \to X$ gives
$$[Y,[Z,X]] = YZX - YXZ - ZXY + XZY, \qquad [Z,[X,Y]] = ZXY - ZYX - XYZ + YXZ .$$
In the sum each of the six products $XYZ, XZY, YZX, ZYX, YXZ, ZXY$ appears once with each sign, so the total is $0$.

blocks.title: Example 1: infinitesimal rotations and the cross product
blocks.body: Show that $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the cross product as bracket, and compute the exponential of an element.
blocks.solution:
For $a = (a_1, a_2, a_3)$ let $\hat{a}$ be the antisymmetric matrix with $\hat{a}v = a \times v$:
$$\hat{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -a_3 & a_2 \\ a_3 & 0 & -a_1 \\ -a_2 & a_1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The map $a \mapsto \hat{a}$ is a linear bijection $\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathfrak{so}(3)$. On basis vectors, $L_x = \hat{e}_1$, $L_y = \hat{e}_2$, $L_z = \hat{e}_3$ satisfy
$$[L_x, L_y] = L_z, \qquad [L_y, L_z] = L_x, \qquad [L_z, L_x] = L_y,$$
exactly matching $e_1 \times e_2 = e_3$ and its cyclic versions. By bilinearity $[\hat{a}, \hat{b}] = \widehat{a \times b}$ for all $a, b$, so the map is a Lie algebra isomorphism. (In particular the cross product satisfies the Jacobi identity.) In physics these are the commutation relations of angular momentum.

For the exponential, let $u$ be a unit vector and $K = \hat{u}$. Then $K^2 v = u \times (u \times v) = (u\cdot v)u - v$, and $K^3 = -K$. Splitting the series into odd and even powers,
$$e^{\theta K} = I + \sin\theta\, K + (1 - \cos\theta) K^2 ,$$
which is the rotation by angle $\theta$ about the axis $u$ (Rodrigues' formula). Every rotation arises this way (by Euler's theorem on [[lie-groups]]), so $\exp\colon \mathfrak{so}(3) \to \mathrm{SO}(3)$ is onto.

blocks.title: Example 2: two groups, one Lie algebra
blocks.body: Show that $\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathfrak{so}(3)$ as real Lie algebras, although the groups $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ and $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ are not isomorphic.
blocks.solution:
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ consists of traceless skew-Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrices, a real space of dimension $3$ with basis $X_k = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_k$, where
$$\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}$$
are the Pauli matrices. They satisfy $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = i\sigma_3$ and $\sigma_2\sigma_1 = -i\sigma_3$, so $[\sigma_1, \sigma_2] = 2i\sigma_3$ and
$$[X_1, X_2] = \left(-\tfrac{i}{2}\right)^2 \cdot 2i\sigma_3 = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_3 = X_3,$$
and cyclically. These are the relations of $L_x, L_y, L_z$, so $X_k \mapsto L_k$ is an isomorphism $\mathfrak{su}(2) \to \mathfrak{so}(3)$.

Yet $\mathrm{SU}(2) \cong S^3$ is simply connected while $\mathrm{SO}(3) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\}$ is not, so the groups differ. The Lie algebra determines the group only near the identity. The double cover $\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathrm{SO}(3)$ from [[lie-groups]] has exactly this isomorphism as its differential.

blocks.title: Example 3: the exponential map need not be onto
blocks.body: Show that $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is not of the form $e^X$ with $X \in \mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{R})$, even though $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is connected.

blocks.title: The Lie correspondence
blocks.body:
Let $G$, $H$ be Lie groups with Lie algebras $\mathfrak{g}$, $\mathfrak{h}$. (Stated without full proof; see the next section.)

1. A Lie group homomorphism $\varphi\colon G \to H$ has a differential $d\varphi\colon \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}$ at the identity, which is a Lie algebra homomorphism, and $\varphi(e^X) = e^{d\varphi(X)}$.
2. If $G$ is connected, $\varphi$ is determined by $d\varphi$.
3. If $G$ is connected and simply connected, every Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{h}$ is $d\varphi$ for a unique Lie group homomorphism $\varphi$.
4. (Lie's third theorem) Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a connected, simply connected Lie group, unique up to isomorphism.

blocks.title: Why the bracket determines the group locally
blocks.body:
Full proofs are in Hall or Lee. Part 2 follows from two facts already met: $\exp$ maps a neighbourhood of $0$ onto a neighbourhood of the identity, and a connected group is generated by any neighbourhood of the identity. Together with part 1, $\varphi$ is known on generators.

The reason the bracket is enough is the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula: for small $X$, $Y$,
$$\log\big(e^X e^Y\big) = X + Y + \tfrac12[X,Y] + \tfrac{1}{12}\big([X,[X,Y]] + [Y,[Y,X]]\big) + \cdots,$$
where every further term is an iterated bracket. So the group law near the identity can be written using only the vector space structure and the bracket of $\mathfrak{g}$.

Some consequences. Classifying connected Lie groups reduces largely to classifying Lie algebras, and representations of a simply connected group are the same as representations of its Lie algebra. Two more theorems, stated without proof. The finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras over $\mathbb{C}$ were classified by Killing and Cartan: four infinite families $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$ $(n \ge 1)$, $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ $(n \ge 2)$, $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$ $(n \ge 3)$, $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}$ $(n \ge 4)$ and five exceptional algebras $\mathfrak{g}_2, \mathfrak{f}_4, \mathfrak{e}_6, \mathfrak{e}_7, \mathfrak{e}_8$. The smallest, $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$, with basis
$$e = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad f = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \quad h = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad [h,e] = 2e,\ [h,f] = -2f,\ [e,f] = h,$$
has, up to isomorphism, exactly one irreducible finite-dimensional representation of each dimension $m+1$, in which $h$ has eigenvalues $m, m-2, \dots, -m$. Through $\mathfrak{su}(2) \otimes \mathbb{C} \cong \mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ this is the classification of quantum spin.

- $e^{X+Y} \ne e^X e^Y$ in general. With $e$ and $f$ as above, $e^e e^f = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $3$, while $e^{e+f}$ has trace $2\cosh 1 \approx 3.086$. The identity holds when $X$ and $Y$ commute.
- The bracket is not associative: in $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, $[\,[L_x, L_x], L_y] = 0$ but $[L_x, [L_x, L_y]] = [L_x, L_z] = -L_y$.
- The exponential map need not be onto (Example 3) or one-to-one ($e^{2\pi J} = e^0 = I$).
- A Lie algebra does not determine a single group: the connected groups with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ are the simply connected one and its quotients by discrete central subgroups. Example 2 is the smallest case.
- Real forms differ: $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{R})$ are not isomorphic as real Lie algebras, although both become $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{C})$ after complexifying.

The matrix exponential is the solution operator of constant-coefficient linear systems on [[ode-systems]] and [[ode-linear]], and it is computed in practice with [[eigen|eigenvalues]] and the [[jordan|Jordan form]]. On a general Lie group, $\mathfrak{g}$ is identified with the left-invariant vector fields and the bracket with the Lie bracket of vector fields from [[smooth-manifolds]]; the Maurer–Cartan form of [[differential-forms]] encodes the same structure. Representations of Lie algebras feed back into the representation theory of compact groups, which extends [[group-representations]], and the group side is on [[lie-groups]].

1. Verify $[h,e] = 2e$, $[h,f] = -2f$ and $[e,f] = h$ for the matrices above.
2. Compute $\exp\begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{pmatrix}$ and interpret it as multiplication by the complex number $e^{a + ib}$.
3. The Heisenberg algebra consists of the strictly upper triangular real $3\times 3$ matrices. Find a basis $x, y, z$ with $[x,y] = z$ and $[x,z] = [y,z] = 0$, and compute $e^{x}e^{y}e^{-x}e^{-y}$ exactly.
4. Show that $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ are not isomorphic. (Hint: in $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb{R})$ the map $Y \mapsto [h, Y]$ has eigenvalues $2, -2, 0$; in $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ every map $Y \mapsto [X,Y]$ has purely imaginary eigenvalues.)

entry.sum: A topology on a set $X$ is a choice of open subsets containing $\varnothing$ and $X$ and closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; a map is continuous when preimages of open sets are open. This keeps exactly the part of a metric that continuity needs. A space is connected when it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets, and continuous images of connected spaces are connected, which is the general form of the intermediate value theorem.
key: f\colon X \to Y \text{ continuous} \iff f^{-1}(V) \text{ is open for every open } V \subseteq Y
X \text{ connected} \iff \text{the only subsets of } X \text{ that are both open and closed are } \varnothing,\ X
A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ connected} \iff A \text{ is an interval}; \qquad X \text{ connected},\ f \text{ continuous} \implies f(X) \text{ connected}
entry.why: Topological spaces are the common setting for continuity in analysis, geometry and algebra, including spaces with no useful metric such as quotient spaces, weak topologies on function spaces and the Zariski topology; invariants like connectedness prove facts such as that the line and the plane are not homeomorphic.

links.note: The intermediate value theorem is the statement that a continuous image of the connected interval $[0,1]$ is connected, and limits and continuity in metric spaces are special cases of the topological notions.
The Zariski topology, whose closed sets are the zero sets of polynomials, is a non-Hausdorff topology that lets geometric language be used for solution sets of polynomial equations.
Weak and weak-* topologies on infinite-dimensional normed spaces are generally not metrisable, so their compactness and convergence properties are stated in terms of open sets.

Armstrong, Basic Topology
Folland, Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications

blocks.body:
On the page on [[metric-spaces]], continuity of a map between metric spaces turns out to have a description that never mentions distance: $f$ is continuous exactly when the preimage of every open set is open. Many different metrics, such as the taxicab, Euclidean and maximum metrics on $\mathbb{R}^2$, have the same open sets and therefore the same continuous maps. For continuity, only the open sets matter.

Topology takes this seriously: a topological space is a set together with a choice of which subsets count as open, subject to three simple rules. This lets us work with spaces that have no natural metric, such as spaces built by gluing (a torus made from a square), spaces of functions, and the Zariski topology of algebraic geometry. The page ends with connectedness and the intermediate value theorem in its general form.

blocks.title: Topological space
Examples
blocks.body:
- Metric topology. In a metric space, call $U$ open if around each of its points it contains some ball $B(x, r)$. This satisfies the three axioms; the finite-intersection rule uses the minimum of finitely many radii, and fails for infinite intersections: $\bigcap_{n \ge 1} (-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n) = \{0\}$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$.
- Equivalent metrics. On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the maximum, Euclidean and taxicab metrics satisfy $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$, so every ball for one contains a concentric ball for each other, and all three give the same topology.
- Discrete topology: every subset is open. Indiscrete topology: only $\varnothing$ and $X$.
- Cofinite topology on an infinite set $X$: the open sets are $\varnothing$ and the sets with finite complement. On $\mathbb{C}$, this is the Zariski topology, whose closed sets are the zero sets of polynomials in one variable.
- Finite examples. On $X = \{a, b\}$ there are exactly four topologies: indiscrete, discrete, $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, X\}$ and $\{\varnothing, \{b\}, X\}$. A three-point set has $29$.
- Subspace topology. If $A \subseteq X$, the open sets of $A$ are the sets $U \cap A$ with $U$ open in $X$. For instance $[0, \tfrac12)$ is open in the subspace $[0,1]$ of $\mathbb{R}$, though not open in $\mathbb{R}$.
- Product topology on $X \times Y$: a set is open if it is a union of "open rectangles" $U \times V$. On $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ this gives the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

blocks.title: Closure and the Hausdorff property
blocks.body:
Let $A \subseteq X$. The closure $\overline{A}$ is the intersection of all closed sets containing $A$ (the smallest closed superset of $A$). A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods.

Every metric space is Hausdorff (use balls of radius half the distance). A cofinite space on an infinite set is not: two nonempty open sets each omit only finitely many points, so they intersect. Without the Hausdorff property sequences behave strangely: in $\mathbb{Z}$ with the cofinite topology, $x_n = n$ converges to every point, since an open set containing $p$ omits only finitely many integers. In general spaces sequences do not even detect closures or continuity, which is why everything here is phrased with open sets.

blocks.title: Lemma: points of the closure
blocks.body: Let $A \subseteq X$ and $x \in X$. Then $x \in \overline{A}$ if and only if every open neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$.

Suppose some open $U

otin \overline{A}$. Conversely, if $x 
otin \overline{A}$ there is a closed $C \supseteq A$ with $x 
otin C$; then $U = X \setminus C$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$ disjoint from $A$.

blocks.title: Continuity and homeomorphism
blocks.body: A map $f\colon X \to Y$ between topological spaces is continuous if $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$. It is a homeomorphism if it is a bijection and both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous. Spaces related by a homeomorphism are topologically identical: the bijection matches their open sets exactly.

blocks.title: Characterisations of continuity

blocks.body:
(1) and (2) are equivalent because $f^{-1}(Y \setminus C) = X \setminus f^{-1}(C)$.

(1) implies (3). Let $x \in \overline{A}$ and let $V$ be an open neighbourhood of $f(x)$. Then $f^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$, so by the lemma it contains a point $a \in A$, and $f(a) \in V \cap f(A)$. Every neighbourhood of $f(x)$ meets $f(A)$, so $f(x) \in \overline{f(A)}$.

(3) implies (2). Let $C \subseteq Y$ be closed and $A = f^{-1}(C)$. Then $f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)} \subseteq \overline{C} = C$, so $\overline{A} \subseteq f^{-1}(C) = A$. Hence $A = \overline{A}$ is closed.

For composites, $(g \circ f)^{-1}(W) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(W))$ is open whenever $W$ is. The equivalence with epsilon–delta continuity for metric spaces is proved on [[metric-spaces]].

blocks.title: Example 1: checking the definitions
blocks.body:
Let $X = \{a, b, c\}$.

1. Is $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b\}, X\}$ a topology on $X$? Is $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$?
2. Let $X_d$ and $X_i$ denote $X$ with the discrete and the indiscrete topology. Which of the identity maps $X_d \to X_i$ and $X_i \to X_d$ is continuous?
3. Show that the map $f\colon [0, 2\pi) \to S^1$, $f(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, is a continuous bijection but not a homeomorphism.
blocks.solution:
1. The first is not a topology: $\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}$ is missing. The second is: it contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, and it is a chain $\varnothing \subseteq \{a\} \subseteq \{a,b\} \subseteq X$, so unions and intersections of its members are again members.

2. $X_d \to X_i$ is continuous, because every subset of $X_d$ is open, so any preimage is open. $X_i \to X_d$ is not: $\{a\}$ is open in $X_d$, and its preimage $\{a\}$ is not open in $X_i$. More open sets in the domain, or fewer in the target, only help continuity.

3. Continuity and bijectivity are clear. The inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$: the set $U = [0, \pi)$ is open in the subspace $[0, 2\pi)$, but $f(U)$, the upper half of the circle including $(1,0)$ and excluding $(-1, 0)$, is not open in $S^1$, since points $(\cos t, \sin t)$ with $t$ slightly less than $2\pi$ are arbitrarily close to $(1,0)$ and not in $f(U)$. So $(f^{-1})^{-1}(U) = f(U)$ is not open. By contrast $h(x) = \tan(\pi(x - \tfrac12))$ is a homeomorphism $(0,1) \to \mathbb{R}$, with continuous inverse $y \mapsto \tfrac12 + \tfrac1\pi\arctan y$; boundedness is not a topological property.

blocks.title: Connectedness
blocks.body:
A space $X$ is connected if it cannot be written as $X = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ open, disjoint and nonempty. Equivalently, the only subsets of $X$ that are both open and closed are $\varnothing$ and $X$. A subset is connected if it is connected in the subspace topology. $X$ is path-connected if for any $x, y \in X$ there is a continuous $\gamma\colon [0,1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, $\gamma(1) = y$.

Connectedness is the precise form of "being in one piece".

blocks.title: Connected subsets of the real line
blocks.body: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected if and only if it is an interval (a set $I$ such that $a, b \in I$ and $a < c < b$ imply $c \in I$). In particular $[0,1]$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are connected.

If $A$ is not an interval, pick $a, b \in A$ and $c \notin A$ with $a < c < b$. Then $A \cap (-\infty, c)$ and $A \cap (c, \infty)$ are disjoint, nonempty, open in $A$, and cover $A$, so $A$ is not connected.

Now let $[0,1] = U \cup V$ with $U, V$ disjoint, nonempty and open in $[0,1]$; we derive a contradiction. Say $0 \in U$. Let $S = \{t \in [0,1] : [0, t] \subseteq U\}$, which contains $0$, and let $s = \sup S$. Note that every $t < s$ lies in $U$, since some element of $S$ exceeds $t$.

Case $s \in U$. As $U$ is open in $[0,1]$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(s - \varepsilon, s + \varepsilon) \cap [0,1] \subseteq U$. Together with $[0, s) \subseteq U$ this gives $[0, s'] \subseteq U$ for $s' = \min(s + \varepsilon/2, 1)$, so $s' \in S$. If $s < 1$ then $s' > s$, contradicting $s = \sup S$. If $s = 1$, then $[0,1] \subseteq U$ and $V$ is empty, a contradiction.

Case $s \in V$. Then $s > 0$ (as $0 \in U$), and since $V$ is open there is $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon \le s$ and $(s - \varepsilon, s] \subseteq V$. But points of $(s - \varepsilon, s)$ are less than $s$, hence in $U$. They would lie in $U \cap V = \varnothing$, a contradiction.

So $[0,1]$ is connected. For a general interval $I$, suppose $I = U \cup V$ is a separation and pick $u \in U$, $v \in V$, say $u < v$. Then $[u,v] \subseteq I$, and $U \cap [u,v]$, $V \cap [u,v]$ would separate $[u, v]$, which is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$ by an affine map. Contradiction.

blocks.title: Continuous images of connected spaces

blocks.body:
Suppose $f(X) = U' \cup V'$ with $U'$, $V'$ disjoint, nonempty and open in $f(X)$, say $U' = U \cap f(X)$ and $V' = V \cap f(X)$ with $U, V$ open in $Y$. Then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ are open in $X$, nonempty, disjoint (a point in both would map into $U' \cap V'$) and cover $X$. This contradicts connectedness of $X$.

For 1, $f(X)$ is a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$, hence an interval, containing $\alpha$ and $\beta$, hence everything between them.

For 2, suppose $X = U \cup V$ is a separation, and pick $x \in U$, $y \in V$ and a path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$. Then $\gamma^{-1}(U)$ and $\gamma^{-1}(V)$ separate $[0,1]$, contradicting the previous theorem.

blocks.title: Connected but not path-connected, and invariants
blocks.body:
The converse of part 2 fails. The topologist's sine curve
$$S = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \le 1\} \cup (\{0\} \times [-1, 1])$$
is connected but not path-connected. Proof sketch: the graph part is path-connected, hence connected, and $S$ is its closure; the closure of a connected set is connected (a separation of the closure would restrict to a separation of the set). But no path joins $(0,0)$ to a point of the graph: approaching the segment, the path would have to follow the graph through infinitely many oscillations between heights $-1$ and $1$, contradicting continuity of its $y$-coordinate at the first time it reaches the segment.

Connectedness, the Hausdorff property and the number of components are preserved by homeomorphisms; such invariants are how one proves two spaces are not homeomorphic (Example 3). The [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] and [[homology]] are far-reaching refinements.

blocks.title: Example 2: the intermediate value theorem at work
blocks.body: Prove that at every moment there are two antipodal points on the equator with exactly the same temperature (assuming temperature varies continuously).
blocks.solution:
Let $T(\theta)$ be the temperature at longitude $\theta$, a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function, and put $g(\theta) = T(\theta) - T(\theta + \pi)$. Then
$$g(\theta + \pi) = T(\theta + \pi) - T(\theta + 2\pi) = -g(\theta).$$
So $g(0)$ and $g(\pi) = -g(0)$ are zero or of opposite signs, and the intermediate value theorem on $[0, \pi]$ gives $\theta_0$ with $g(\theta_0) = 0$: the points at $\theta_0$ and $\theta_0 + \pi$ have the same temperature.

blocks.title: Example 3: the line is not the plane
blocks.body: Prove that $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$ are not homeomorphic, and more strongly that there is no continuous injective map $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$.
blocks.solution:
Removing a point disconnects the line: $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{c\} = (-\infty, c) \cup (c, \infty)$ is a separation. Removing a point $p$ from the plane does not: any two points of $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ can be joined by a path consisting of at most two line segments that avoids $p$ (if the segment between them passes through $p$, go instead via any point $z$ off the line through them; the two segments meet that line only at their endpoints), so $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ is path-connected and hence connected.

Now suppose $f\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous and injective. Its image $I$ is connected, hence an interval, with more than one point. An interval has at most two endpoints, so we can choose $p$ with $c = f(p)$ not an endpoint of $I$. By injectivity the connected set $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ maps onto $I \setminus \{c\}$, which is not an interval and hence disconnected. Contradiction. A homeomorphism would be such a map, so $\mathbb{R} \not\cong \mathbb{R}^2$.

blocks.body:
- "Not open" does not mean "closed". In $\mathbb{R}$, $[0,1)$ is neither; $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both. A space is connected precisely when $\varnothing$ and $X$ are the only sets that are both.
- Openness is relative ($[0, \tfrac12)$ is open in $[0,1]$, not in $\mathbb{R}$), and a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism (Example 1).
- Continuous maps need not send open sets to open sets: $x \mapsto x^2$ sends $(-1,1)$ to $[0,1)$. Continuity is about preimages.
- Connected does not imply path-connected (topologist's sine curve), though for open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ the two notions agree.

The next basic notion is [[compactness]]: continuous images of compact spaces are compact, and together with connectedness this gives the extreme value theorem. Quotient topologies build new spaces by gluing, leading to [[classification-of-surfaces|the classification of surfaces]], and the [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] detects holes that connectedness cannot see. Spaces that look locally like $\mathbb{R}^n$ with smooth transition maps are [[smooth-manifolds]]. Topological spaces and continuous maps form the category $\mathbf{Top}$, a basic example on [[categories-functors]]. Infinite-dimensional [[normed-spaces|normed spaces]] carry weak topologies given by no metric.

1. Show that in the cofinite topology on an infinite set every one-point set is closed, yet the space is not Hausdorff.
2. Show that $\mathbb{Q}$, as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$, is totally disconnected: its only nonempty connected subsets are single points.
3. Show that the circle $S^1$ is not homeomorphic to any interval of $\mathbb{R}$. (Remove a point.)
4. Prove that $f\colon X \to Y$ is continuous if and only if for every $x \in X$ and every open $V \ni f(x)$ there is an open $U \ni x$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$.

def count(n):
  X=frozenset(range(n))
  subs=[frozenset(s) for r in range(n+1) for s in itertools.combinations(range(n),r)]
  c=0
  for mask in range(1<<len(subs)):

    if frozenset() not in T or X not in T: continue

T=lambda s: 3*sin(s)+cos(2*s)+sin(3*s+1)
g=T(t)-T(t+pi)
assert simplify(g.subs(t,t+pi)+g)==0
import math
Tf=lambda s: 3*math.sin(s)+math.cos(2*s)+math.sin(3*s+1)
gf=lambda s: Tf(s)-Tf(s+math.pi)
a,b=0.0,math.pi
assert gf(a)*gf(b)<0
for _ in range(60):
  m=(a+b)/2
  if gf(a)*gf(m)<=0: b=m
  else: a=m
assert abs(gf(a))<1e-9
